Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. There was a reference by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) yesterday to a 'special train' or 'express train.' I may say that a reference of that kind has been made previously in this House. I happened to meet the

hon. member this morning, and I told him it was my intention to ask him for an explanation. I thought the remarks were directed to me. I asked yesterday if I was correct in thinking so, and the hon. gentleman replied that he had directed his remarks to me. I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat, hut I see there is another sinner on the other side, and perhaps I may be able to get some information from him-

Mr. CONMEE

he having used the
same language. I refer to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster).
Order.
I think the word 'sinner' should not be employed in the debate.
I will withdraw that word, and I will refer to the hon. member as the spotless dove that represents North Toronto.
Do I understand that the opprobious epithet has been withdrawn?

I may say to the House that I am indebted to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) himself for this word, he having applied the same name to me last year. If he wishes to deny that he is spotless and wants us to assume that he has spots all over him, I can tell him of some of them
I think I must ask you, Mr. Speaker, to keep the hon gentleman (Mr. Conmee) to the point. Surely, we are not going to have a bear garden again.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) has risen to a question of privilege, and he must confine himself to that question.
May I ask the hon. gentleman for an explanation of his remarks in regard to this 'special train'-what relation he supposes me to have to that subject, and why he used the expression in the House?
What remarks?
A few evenings ago the hon. member used the same expression, 'Send him away on his special train'-
I think the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) had better confine himself to the present debate.

Very well. I see two or three members on the other side who indulged in a good deal of mirth over this question. I think they nearly all clapped their desks. Among them, for instance, was my venerable friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). Surely, he will give me an explanation; surely he will condescend to give me some information with regard to this particular train.
How can they give information when they had nothing to do with it?
I think I saw the gallant colonel (Mr. Hughes) also

I would like to ask the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) a question: How can any one on this side give information concerning that train when the hon. gentleman himself seems to be the only one posted concerning it?

I assumed that the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) had the courage of his convictions, but it seems that he indulges in remarks at the expense of his fellow members and, when asked for an explanation, has none to give.
Order.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) had better confine himself to the question of privilege.
I see that the hon. member for Simcoe, who used the words of which I have spoken, is now in his seat. Perhaps he would be good enough to give an explanation of what he referred to.
The hon. member refers to
Order.
The hon. member has referred to 'the member for Simcoe.' I am one of the members from Simcoe, and I do not wish to be catechised by the hon. gentleman, as I said nothing concerning the matter.
I do not think the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie) had any idea that he was referred to. I referred to the hon. member for East Simcoe.
He is on your own side.
South Simcoe. Let us have it 'South.'

I see the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) is now in his seat. I ask him if the remarks he made with regard to 'special train' or 'express train' were directed to myself. I would like an explanation from him now as to why he coupled me with that transaction.

I had not the advantage of being in the Chamber at the time the hon. gentleman began his remarks; I understand him, however, to refer to something that I interjected across the floor of the House yesterday. When the hon. member from Rainy River spoke of an accommodation affidavit, I said it was not an accommodation train, nor was it a special train, nor was it, I might say, a Sunday ' nighter ' either. The train I referred to was a Sunday night train-if I recollect correctly- whether the hon. gentleman had any con-

nection with that train I am not prepared to say. If it is in order, I would like to elaborate more fully what I did refer to. I referred to an incident that occurred in connection with the last general election on a certain Sunday night previous to the Monday of the election. A certain train started from Port Arthur, I think, for a bush poll, and that bush poll was in the hon. gentleman's riding where an attempt was being made to conduct a special and peculiar election in the hon. gentleman's interest. A number of young and inexperienced, and I am afraid, somewhat ignorant boys were upon that train, were got upon that train, and they were taken to that poll; and the sworn evidence in the court of justice was that these young men, or some of them, voted several times, and voted, if I recollect the evidence rightly, in the interest of my hon. friend from Rainy River. The incident was a very disgraceful and unfortunate one, and it reflected no credit upon the manner of conducting elections in the Dominion of Canada. It was a special train, and_ it had the distinguished honour of having a very distinguished name applied to it, ' the Conmee special.'

I expected just such an explanation from my hon. friend. He is entirely misinformed as to the facts. He has not hesitated to make insinuations which I cannot help but think reflect upon me, because the hon. gentleman wished to convey that there was some wrong-doing on my part in connection with a special train during the last election. Now he has made to the House a statement which, to use parliamentary language, is entirely incorrect. I happen to have in my possession a little bit of evidence on that point to which the hon. member referred.
I think it would be an abuse of the privilege of the House to introduce that evidence. The hon. gentleman may properly make a statement now.

I am not going to attempt to give the evidence further than to say that there was no evidence of anv special train. Perhaps I may be permitted to Tead the words which the'judge used in his address to the jury. The judge, in addressing the jury in regard to this matter, called their attention to the fact
What is the name of the judge?

Judge Britton. I have in my hand the official report; anybody is welcome to see it. He said that reference had been made to a special train, and he called their attention to the fact that there was no evidence, that nobody had given any evidence, that there was a special train; nobody pretended to say there was a special
train. The judge, for the benefit of the jury, defined a special train; he said it was a train engaged for a special purpose, to start from a specific point. The train in question was a construction train, a usual construction train used in the construction of all railways. This was a Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, or the branch from Fort William west. The line was not then completed ; it was not opened for traffic. Everybody who wished to go on that line, either for election purposes or for any other, took advantage of the train, the work train going out at a certain hour on that evening. The evidence goes to show, not only that some voters did go-that is true-but a great many others went on that train. The train carried supplies for track laying, coal and other things for the work, just as it did on other occasions. There was nothing special about it. Now, I notice that some hon. gentlemen seem to be very much interested in this particular train. Let me say to them that there is nothing to their credit in the case that came before the courts, and nothing to the discredit of the member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River. No person ever suggested that I had anything to do with it, or any knowledge of it, or the slightest thing to do with regard to it. I do not propose to discuss the evidence now, but it goes to show that there was a prostitution of justice, manipulated by a government other than the government that forms this cabinet.
Order.
Those words exceed the limit of debate.
I think I am trying to keep within the rules of debate.
I refer to the words 'prostitution of justice.' I invite the hon. gentleman to withdraw them.

I will change them, and say there was a miscarriage of justice. There was one man in connection with that transaction-I do not want to mention names, it is not fair-but I have no hesitation in doing so if hon. gentlemen wish me to do so. The culprit in the whole case, as the evidence showed, and as the jury found, was the brother of the Conservative organizer in that particular riding.
The question of privilege of course relates to the hon. gentleman himself, and he should not depart from that point.
I think Mr. Speaker, you should compel the hon. member for Rainy River to take his seat when you are giving a ruling.

An hon. member has a right to make an explanation, because the

hon. member for Simooe (Mr. Lennox) stated that there was a fraudulent transaction in connection with that poll, that a special train was the Conmee special. I say these words are untrue, they are entirely incorrect, and I ask the hon. member to withdraw them.
I rise to a point of order. In the first place I did not say there was a special train, I said it had been spoken of as a special train, as the Conmee special.
The House has heard the words , of the hon. gentleman, and surely when that question is raised
The hon. gentleman is bound to accept the statement of the hon. member for Simcoe as to what words he did use. That is the rule of the House.
I do not see that his present words make it much better.

It is the rule of the House. The hon. gentleman is bound to accept the statement of the hon. member he is referring to the moment he says, 'These are the words which I uttered.' That is the rule of the House.
But, Mr. Speaker, have I not a right to object to the words if they are not correct?
You must accept his statement of the words that he used.

I bow to your ruling. The hon. member now says that what he said was that the train was spoken of as a special train, as the Conmee train. I say that is equally objectionable, because it casts a reflection upon me. The hon. member went further than that, he referred to the personation of votes, and he said they were all cast for me. The evidence does not show that; the evidence shows that votes were cast for both candidates.
I rise to a point of order, I did not say that the votes were all cast for my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee).

The hon. gentleman made the statement that the votes were cast for me. Whether he used the word ' all ' or not, I am not going to say but he did .make the statement that the votes were cast for me. That statement is incorrect and I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw it.
I do not understand the hon. member's point.
No, nor nobody else, I think.

The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in his remarks stated that this poll was a bush poll, that Mr. CONMEE.
a train was got up on Sunday after evening to take the voters there. The whole tenor of the hon. gentleman's remarks was that this was a manipulation, a wrongful manipulation under the law, a disgrace to the elections in the country.
So he said.
Hear, hear.
That the illegal votes that were cast were cast for myself as the candidate.
In your interest.
In my interest. Now I say that is not the evidence

That is the evidence.
Mr. CONMEE-but the evidence disclosed was that there were at that poll improper votes but that they were cast for both candidates. The hon. member has made a statement that he should withdraw and I ask that he do withdraw it.

I cannot compel the hon. member to withdraw any statement; I have not read the evidence. It is a matter of appreciation on one side or the other. The hon. member has made a statement, he has denied a statement made by the hon. member on the other side, and I think the question of privilege does not arise.

On the Order:
Further consideration of the motion of Mr. Fieding, that the Speaker leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply.

I want to draw attention to the fact that this order is improperly on the Order Paper. It was superseded by the adjournment of the House, it was an undisposed-of motion and should not appear on the Order Paper as it is. Bourinot refers to a similar motion as follows :
On another occasion the House adjourned while a motion for the Speaker to leave the Chair was under consideration, and it became necessary on the next sitting day to move that the House do immediately resolve itself in Committee.
As I understand and interpret the rules a motion falls to the ground and must be renewed under such circumstances and therefore this order is improperly on the Order Paper.

Since Bourinot wrote his work, the House in 1906 adopted a new series of rules. Rule 32 reads:
If at the hour of six o'clock, p.m., on a Wednesday or Thursday, or at the time of the adjournment of the House, a motion on the notice paper he under consideration, that question shall stand first on the order of the following day, next after orders to which a special precedence has been assigned by rule or order of the House.
I have consulted the officials of the House in this matter and from what I can learn this rule is susceptible of two interpretations. I am giving it now the most favourable interpretation and allowing the question to Temain on the Order Paper. As the rule here evidently requires, in spirit if not in letter, I have allowed the motion to remain on the Order Paper and I think it is now in order.

speechtext:
If you, Mr. Speaker, and the House will pardon me, I have a statement to make to the House with regard to the objection I raised yesterday. You remember I stated yesterday that if my hon.
friend would produce to the House the original affidavit which was declared or sworn to upon the 12th of October, 1908, I Would make no objection! to the reading of the whole of it. This morning I had the opportunity of having a conference with my hon. friend the member from St. John (Mr. Daniel) and he has undertaken to produce and file with the clerk - which I presume would be done before I make any observations to the House-the original declaration sworn to or declared upon the 12th of October. Upon that undertaking of my hon. friend I withdraw all objection to the reading of the declaration which was made at a later date.

I am very glad to hear the statement of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). I stated yesterday that I had the original affidavit in my possession, and I was only anxious to lay it before any committee which this House would appoint.
It is to be laid on the table, is the understanding with my hon. friend,-and filed with the clerk of the House. Is there any misunderstanding between us as to that?
I have no objection at all to take that course.
Very well.

And I will have much pleasure, after reading it, in placing it in the hands of the clerk of this House. I am very glad indeed to hear the statement of the Minister of Public Works. I think the stand which he has taken to-day is one not only in his own interest but in that of the public life of Canada generally.
I never objected to that.

When these charges are made and solemly declared and sworn to in various parts of the country I certainly think, especially when they affect a person so high up in the country as a minister of the Crown, that the least parliament can do is to investigate these charges to see whether they are true or whether they are false.
May I interject a question?
Only with the consent of the hon. member who has the floor.

With the hon. gentleman's permission, are we to understand that there is any procedure taking place to-day different from what would necessarily take place under the rules of parliament? As I understand, when a member reads a document in the House it must be laid on the table.

As I understand there are two declarations, one declaration which was made and signed, or rather alleged to have been made and signed, on the lgth October, 1908. My hon. friend says he has that declaration with him. That is a declaration which I have for months been seeking to obtain access to. My hon. friend has undertaken now that that declaration shall be filed with the clerk of the House
My hon. friend has stated he has also in his possession another declaration which makes a slight change in the previous one, and declared to in the month of March of the present year. That is the one my hon. friend is going to read and that is the one which in the ordinary course will be laid on the table. But my hon. friend has also undertaken that he will also lay on the table a declaration which was originally made or declared to on the 12th of October, 1908.

Will the House allow me for a moment. I wish to guard the House against a possible error. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) stated not once, not twice, but three times that he had the original affidavit and that was the affidavit he proposed to read, and was only too anxious to have read.

I have not only the affidavit referred to but I also have the other affidavit which so far has not been referred to, and made by Mr. Gershon S. Mayes, I think the day following the original affidavit.
Don't let my hon. friend misunderstand me; surely there is no need of misunderstanding.
There is not any.

There was an affidavit or declaration professed to have been made by Mr. Mayes on the 12th of October, 1908. That declaration is alleged to have been read at a meeting in St. John. It was published in the St. John press upon the morning of the 13th, and was published broadcast throughout Canada the same morning. It must have been telegraphed to the various newspapers, the Conservative newspapers particularly, throughout Canada. Now, that is the declaration which I understand my hon. friend has with him and which he has undertaken to file with the Clerk of this House. I am quite willing he should read the other upon that undertaking, and then of course they will both be filed, but don't let my hon. friend misunderstand what I say.

I have been making great efforts to get this affidavit before the House, and I leave it to the judgment of the House if it is my fault that I have been prevented. Perhaps I should go over it all again.
Hear, hear.
I don't want to do that,- because I purpose laying a motion before the House and in that motion there are extracts from the affidavit.
Read it all.

Very well, I will read it all:-
I, Gershon S. Mayes, of the parish of Lancaster, city and county of St. John, province T New Brunswick, contractor, do solemnly declare:-That on the first day of September, 1905, on the advice of the Hon. Wm. Pugsley, who was then Attorney General of the province of New Brunswick, and is now Minister cf Public Works of Canada, I had a conversation with George McAvity, of the city of St. John, and the said province, merchant, relative to tenders for dredging which was then to be done in the harbour of St. John by the Public Works Department of Canada, of which the Hon. C. S. Hyman was then minister. Mr. iMcAvity proposed that I should go to Ottawa on Monday the 4th of September as he was going and would meet me there at the Russell House on the 5th inst. We did meet according to appointment. Mr. McAvity wanted to know what price I wanted. I told him that I had tendered in June for 50 cents per cubic yard. He said: Why not ask 55 cents, giving him (McAvity) five cents per yard or 10 per cent. I said: Why not do as we talked of in St. John, which was that he should go in with me and take a quarter or half of the cost of the dredge and receive his proportion of the profits. He said: Yes he could do that when he got home and might put from $10,000 to $20,000 in it and perhaps get some friends in it with him, but for the present he would go in on a percentage basis and would see Hyman right away. Well, I said: What should I do about financing it and wrhat was he going to do to help me? Oh, he said, he could easily arrange with the banks, no trouble at all when you have got the contract. We went to see Hyman at half past two p.m. McAvity went in and I stayed outside. I had told Mr. McAvity to arrange if possible to have at least 400,000 yards to diedge. McAvity came out and got me to go in and I explained to Mr. Hyman the difficulty of bringing a big plant and only digging a small quantity. Mr. Hyman agreed to see that if I got the contract, that is, if I was the lowest tenderer, I should receive the 4GO.OOO yards. Afterwards Mr. McAvity said that I had better arrange an agreement. I said: Why not wait until we get back to St. John and hear whether the tender has been accepted or no-t. He said that he had a copy of agreement already. I said: How did he get it? He said: Oh they were all ready here. I then read it over and told him that it was all one-sided, I was to do the work; he was to get the profit. Well he said: What do you want me to do? I told him that I still thought he should be financially interested, he and his friends, to the extent of from $20,000 to $30,000 at least; that it was a long, back load for me to carry. Oh, he said as before, the banks would help me and wait till I got home. rNo, I said,' 'I have got to go right to Boston and close the trade with the dredge-owners.' 'Well', he said: 'Better sign the agree-

ment now. 'Well', I said: 'Why not you be bound to do something'. Well, he said for me to write something at the bottom and he would sign it. I said: 'I am not a lawyer'. Oh, go ahead', was the reply. So I wrote what came to mind and he signed it. A copy of this agreement is hereto annexed marked ' A ' and the part written by me is marked ' Al.' Now, the affidavit which I have read perhaps places in as succinct a form as I could do it the various statements which have been laid before the public. The statetments, in short, are to this effect, that in June, 1905, Mr. Mayes sent in a tender to the Public Works Department offering to do certain dredging in the city of St. John. The price which he asked for that dredging was 49 cents per cubic yard.
He swears to fifty cents.
Forty-nine.
No sir, he says fifty in the declaration.
I am aware that Mr. Mayes spoke of it as fifty cents and I am aware also that the hon. Minister of Public Works, in this House, a few days ago, spoke of it as fifty cents.
I spoke of it as forty-nine cents.
It has been spoken of a3 a fifty cent contract.
I spoke of it as forty-nine in the return which I gave.

The minister also spoke of it as fifty cents. It is very easy to turn it up. I looked it up on purpose to see whether the minister had made that reference or not and I am absolutely sure I am stating what is correct and that ' Hansard ' will bear me out. That first tender has been carelessly spoken of by every one almost as a 50 cents tender, but in reality it was a 49 cents tender for that class of material and was not accepted by the Department of Public Works. Mr. Mayes, however, was anxious to get a contract with the government, so he looked around for help and applied to my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), who was then, I believe, his solicitor and also Attorney General of New Brunswick, and he advised Mr. Mayes to consult Mr. Geo. McAvity. In that, there was nothing out of the way that I can see. Mr. McAvity was then, as he is now, a prominent business man in the city of St. John, financially able in every way. Mr. McAvity, however, also occupied the position of active business manager of, or the hub around which the whole Liberal party machine in the city of St. John turned. In that statement, I think I am entirely within the truth, because it is well known by every one in that city that Mr. McAvity was the chief executive administrator, so to speak, of the Liberal party in St. John at that time and is still, for all I know. Mr. Mayes took the advice of his solicitor (Mr. Pugsley) and consulted Mr. McAvity, with the result that they both came to Ottawa. They had a consultation here about the prices to be charged for this dredging. Mr. McAvity interviewed' Hon. Mr. Hyman, who was then Minister of Public Works, and afterwards interviewed Mr. Mayes; and on the strength of those interviews, Mr. Mayes put in a tender at 55 cents. Then he was asked by Mr. McAvity to sign an agreement to pay him five cents per yard over and above what he had told Mr. McAvity he was willing to do the work for. He signed that agreement. But Mr. Mayes, although he signed that agreement. was not entirely satisfied with it. He thought it was altogether one-sided, that under it he was to do the work and Mr. McAvity was to get the profit. He therefore urged the latter to take a financial interest in this dredging, but Mr. McAvity _ would not consent to do so and did not. If it were necessary to give any proof of that, I might refer to the affidavit which Mr. McAvity himself made and published in the city of St. John as a reply to the affidavit of Mr. Mayes. But I do not think it necessary, because it is generally known that Mr. McAvity had no financial interest whatever in

that dredge and did not claim any. Consequently the only interest he had in the matter was in the obtaining of this percentage on the money paid Mr. Mayes for the dredging; and what Mr. Mayes got in exchange for that five per cent was the political influence of Mr. McAvity with the Department of Public Works. That agreement, 1 submit, is something which this parliament has the right to take seriously into its consideration and ought to deal with. All that Mr. McAvity had to give or to sell in connection with this dredging contract was his influence with the Department of Public Works. He makes no claim to have any financial interest whatever in the dredging plank In fact, according to Mr. Mayes, he declined to take any financial interest in the matter at all. All he gave was his political influence, so that, under these circumstances, the agreement between Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes was, I submit, a corrupt and immoral one. I think I am justified in going further and saying that it was an illegal agreement. If hon. gentlemen will look up section 158 of the Criminal Code, subsection (1), they will find it is as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine of not less than $100, and not exceeding $1,000, and to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not less than one month; and in default of payment of such fine, to imprisonment for a further term not exceeding six months who, by reason of, or under pretense of, possessing influence with the government, or with any minister or official thereof, demands, exacts or receives from any person any compensation, fee or reward, for procuring from the government the payment of any claim, or any portion thereof or for procuring or furthering the appointment of himself or any other person to any office, place or employment, or for procuring, furthering the obtaining for himself, or any other person, any grant, lease or other benefit from the government ; or offers, promises or pays to such person, under the circumstances and for the causes aforesaid, or any of them, any such compensation, fee or reward.
N-ow, I make no claim at all to be learned in the law; but looking at that section as an ordinary layman, it appears to me that such an agreement as the one I have mentioned must come under the clause I have read. Therefore, I think I am justified in declaring that that agreement was not only corrupt and immoral but also illegal.
From what I can see, it appears to me that this $35,933, which was paid to Mr. McAvity under this agreement, was nothing but plain plunder of the public purse and undisguised robbery of the public treasury.
I do not intend troubling the House with any extracts from newspapers, although there was a great deal published in connection with this matter, except to refer to an editorial in a St. John Liberal newspaper, edited by a man well known in public life, who has always been a consistent Liberal,
who is so constant to his Liberal principles that even when he held the office of postmaster, while his party were out of office and the Conservative party were in power, that newspaper still stood by its Liberal principles and criticised the government of the day, although its proprietor and editor was an official under the Conservative administration. And he afterwards resigned his position and gave up whatever financial emoluments he was receiving from it rather than give up anything of his Liberal convictions. The paper I refer to is the St. John * Globe,' and in its issue of October 16, 1908, the following editorial appears:
Thirty-five Thousand Dollars.
While the air is blue with affidavits, declarations and letters in regard to the dredging transactions between Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity, and while there are several statements and counter statements, there is danger of having one important matter overlooked. That important matter is that the Dominion of Canada is out over thirty-five thousand dollars upon the Mayes dredging contract, and that, apparently, somebody ought to pay that sum of money back to the Dominion treasury. It really belongs to the people of Canada; and indeed the sum may be more than the amount named. The former Minister of Public Works-Mr. Hyman-Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity would seem to be the principal parties concerned. Mr. Mayes was willing to undertake to do the work of dredging for fifty cents a yard, and tendered to do it for that price in June, 1905. Apparently this price was for a smaller quantity of dredging than was eventually done. And the natural inference is that if Mr. Mayes could dredge a smaller quantity at fifty cents a yard, the much larger quantity which he eventually had assigned to him could have been done at a lower price. However, that is not material. Nothing came of the June tenders, but early in September of that year Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes were in Ottawa together and Mr. Mayes got the enlarged quantity of dredging at a higher price per yard-five cents more-than he originally offered to do the work for. There is no clear indication at all why Mr. Hyman allowed the higher rate, but possibly he may not have given the matter much thought, or have regarded the increase per yard as not very serious. It is quite clear now that if he took this simple view of the matter he was in error, for it enabled Mr. Mayes to pay Mr. McAvity a very large sum out of the profits of his work, over, as we have stated, thirty-five thousand dollars. As it would be unreasonable as regards Mr. Hyman to assume that he knew of the arrangement between Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes, it would be unfair to assume that he ought to make good out of his own means the higher price paid out of the treasury to Mr. Mayes. This leaves the matter as between Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity on the one part and the Canadian people, whose money they got, on the other part. Mr. McAvity is not very clear in his statement as to why Mr. Mayes should pay him the amount which he did pay him, although he does seem to have done some service in going to Ottawa several times in connection with Mr. Mayes's business. Mr. COMMONS
Mayes, capable business man as he is assumed to be, seems not to know clearly why he paid the thirty-five thousand dollars over to Mr, McAvity, and asserts that he has taken proceedings at law to get it back. If he gets it back, it ought surely to be returned to the Canadian people to whom it would seem in equity to really belong. But, perhaps, if Mr. McAvity were to send the money back to the treasury, and Mr. Mayes were to stop his suits to recover it, that would seem to be the best settlement. Hon. Mr. Pugsley, who is now the Minister of Public Works, standing in the interests of the people, would certainly do the right thing in endeavouring to secure some such settlement in the interests of the country, for it appears to he quite clear now without any reflection upon his predecessor's management then .that Mr. Mayes could have done the work for the price at which he first tendered. After all is said

I would ask the special attention of the Eight Hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to this:
After all is said, the main consideration is the public welfare, and the safeguarding of the interests of the people whose money has been so improperly taken from them. This whole matter is a vivid illustration of how the people may he preyed upon. A crisis will come in the administration of affairs in this country if there he not close attention given to the real interests of the people.

Let me ask my hon. friend to tell us, after he has thought it all over, what he meant by calling up the case of my hon. friend who now so worthily represents the county of Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) in my own province; what was the sense of my hon. friend referring to that case, also making a suggestion as to the duty of the right hon. the Prime Minister in the circumstances? Now, I desire to repeat the well known rule, I repeat it for the information of my hon. friend from the city of St. John, that if a member of parliament desires to have a minister's conduct investigated, if he thinks the minister	has	been guilty of	any	wrong-doing,then	it	is not only	the	proper andmanly course, but the parliamentary course, the course which appeals to the	good	judgment of	all	decent men,that	he	should have	the	courage to
prefer his charge before the House and undertake the responsibility of producing ground for his charge. That is a fair course to take towards a minister, and it is the course which I am sure, upon reflection, the hon. gentleman will see he should have pursued.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to call attention to some further false statements in the affidavit or declaration which my hon. friend has read. It makes the statement that Mr. Mayes was informed that he was the only tenderer upon both occasions; and my hon.

friend in fathering that affidavit, in making himself responsible
I wish to correct the hon. minister. I am not the father of that affidavit.
Well, I am sure the hon. gentleman is not the stepfather.
Perhaps he is the dry nurse.

That may be. At all events, my hon. friend does assume a certain responsibility, in fact a large measure of responsibility, for any affidavit which he submits to this House. Now no member of parliament should allow people lightly to make affidavits, take them up and read them to this House, where they reflect upon the character of either private citizens or members of parliament. Therefore when a member of this House does read to parliament an affidavit and asks parliament to take certain action upon it, his action ought to be a guarantee that he has made some inquiries to satisfy himself as to the truth of the statements which are there made. Now, what has my hon. friend done? He has read to this House, in the first place, an affidavit which it was admitted at the time it was read to the public meeting, contained a false statement of a most material character, and which continued to contain that false statement down to the 24th of March of the present year, an affidavit which neither Mr. Hazen nor anybody else could alter, except Mr. Mayes himself, by taking it back and going before the notary before whom it was sworn, and correcting it and re-swearing to it. He has read here an affidavit which states that Mr. Mayes was the only tenderer on both occasions. Yet my hon. friend knew from the statement which was brought down to this House, or if he did not know he ought to have known it, a statement brought down in answer to a question put by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), that so far from Mr. Mayes being the only tenderer, upon both occasions there were two tenderers, and that he was the lowest upon both occasions. Now, what does my hon. friend think of that? Does he think that is honorable and fair?
I will tell the hon. gentleman what I think of it. I ask him to recollect what was stated in that affidavit with regard to that matter; Mr Mayes says that he was informed months afterwards.
Oh, oh.

You can 'oh, oh,' as much as you like, I am stating what I have just read in that affidavit, and it should be in the memory of every one listening to me now. He does not state that he was the only tenderer, he says that he heard months afterwards that he was the only tenderer.

If it were not for the information from the department before this House, would anybody suppose for a moment but that Mr. Mayes was the only tenderer? Would anybody suppose for a moment but that he intended to convey the impression that he was the only tenderer, and had got this contract at his own price? and that without any further tenders being received, Mr Hyman, the then Minister of Public Works, had awarded him this contract-without having any other tenders between which and his a comparison could be made? Surely the position which my hon. friend has taken in reading this affidavit is very different from the actual position. He puts it forward in this affidavit as if on each occasion there had been no other tenderers, and that this arrangement had been made between him and the Minister of Public Works. Surely the position is very different, because we find that early in the summer of 1905 there were tenders called for, and the specifications contained the condition that the tenderer should own a dredge registered at the time in Canada; we find that there were two tenders received, that the tender of Mr. Mayes for ordinary material was 49 cents per cubic yard, and the next tender, which was that of Messrs. M. J. Haney and Roger Miller, of Toronto, who were prepared to comply with the condition, and who named the price of $3.50 per cubic yard of material described as class 1, and $1.25 per cubic yard for material described as class 2. There you have experienced contractors, the firm of Haney & Miller, of Toronto, tendering to do this work at the price of $1.25 per yard for ordinary material. Now at that time, if the Minister of Public Works had chosen to waive the condition with regard to dredges, and given the contract to Mr. Mayes, there being that great difference between them, I suppose possibly he could have done so, but it would not have been a fair discharge of his duty as Minister of Public Works, because in asking for tenders he had attached a condition as a result of which, of the two tenders, only one was by parties who were prepared to comply with the condition, and that was for a price considerably higher than the Minister of Public Works thought the work was fairly worth. Now then, did he do the right thine in calling again for tenders? I submit he did. He found that the only firm which was prepared to tender for this work and which had a dredge registered in Canada, tendered at a price which he thought in the public interest he ought not to pay, and thinking that the price was excessive, he called again for tenders. That it seems to me was what it was his duty to do. So far as the affidavit shows, so far as any statement my hon. friend has made to the House shows, up to the time, at all events, of calling for new tenders, there was nothing which could be impugned in the conduct of

the Minister of Public Works, or of the officials of the department. Now, he called again for new tenders, and upon the second occasion, it is not true, as Mr. Mayes suggests, that he was the only tenderer. Again tenders were received from Messrs. Haney & Miller, of Toronto, and also from Mr. Mayes, and upon this occasion Mr. Mayes altered his tender for material of class 1. He reduced that. From this affidavit you would suppose that he did nothing but increase his tender, but as a matter of fact he reduced his tender in respect of one kind of material, of which it was supposed and afterwards proved there were large quantities in the harbour of St. John, that is large boulders. He reduced his tender on this class of material from $8.90 to $8.60 per cubic yard, and raised his price on the other material by 6 cents, making it 55 cents a cubic yard. For one class of work, large boulders, he reduced his tender by 30 cents, and for other materials he increased it by 6 cents, and his tender went in in that form. The affidavit read by my hon. friend shows and the records of the department conclusively prove that his tender and that of Messrs. Haney & Miller, of Toronto, went in in the regular way in accordance with the rules of the department. When the tenders were opened it was found that the tender of Messrs. Haney & Miller was $3.75 per cubic yard for materials of class 1 and $1 per cubic yard for material of class 2. Thus there was a difference of 45 cents per cubic yard between the tender of Mr. Mayes and the tender of Messrs. Haney & Miller.
In the face of the departmental record, in the face of the fact that there were these two tenders, I ask what justification can be given by my hon. friend for reading to this House an affidavit which would lead the members of this House and the people of Canada to believe that no tender was submitted upon the second occasion but the tender of Gershon S. Mayes.
Was the specification the same on each occasion when tenders were called for?

The tenders in both cases were the same except that when they were called for early in the summer a provision was inserted that the tenderer must have a dredge registered in Canada and when they were called for in September that stipulation was omitted. In all other respects the tenders were the same. No tenders for what the Minister considered a fair price could be got for the work with that provision in as the tender of Messrs. Haney & Miller had shown, but, in order to meet competition when that condition was done away with, Messrs. Haney & Miller, who are very experienced contractors, tendered at the price of $1 a yard and the tender of Mr. Mayes was 55 cents a yard.
I ask what was the duty of the Minister 137
of Public Works? He had invited new tenders by public advertisement in the various newspapers which would come to the notice of contractors. Two tenders were put in, one from an experienced firm, at $1.00 for ordinary material and the other from Mr. Mayes at 55 cents for the same class of material. What was the duty of the minister? Was it not to accept the lowest tender? My hon. friend will say that having invited new tenders it was the duty of the Minister of Public Works to go to Mr. Mayes and say: Why, you tendered before at 49 cents, although now, in response to a public advertisement, you are the lowest tenderer, although you are 45 cents per cubic yard below the next tenderer, a firm of experienced contractors, yet I will not give you this contract on your tender, you must come down to the lower price. Was it the duty of the Minister of Public Works to do that? I do not think so. Bear in mind that Mr. Mayes in this extraordinary affidavit, prepared and read under extraordinary circumstances on the eve of a general election, when there would be a desire to put forth everything which could be put forth against the department in order to injure the Liberal party, nowhere ventures to insinuate that Mr. Hyman was informed of Mr. Mayes' readiness to tender at 50 cents per cubic yard. Nor does he venture to insinuate that he ever intimated to Mr. Hyman that he would accept less than 55 cents per cubic yard. All he says is that he went to Mr. Hyman and asked if he could have this larger quantity because he said he was going to buy a dredge in the United States which would cost a large sum of money and he wanted to be sure of a large contract, which was not unreasonable. What did Mr. Hyman say, according to Mr. Mayes' own statement? Mr. Hyman immediately said:	'You will get such a
quantity provided you are the lowest tenderer, that is all.' He happened to be the lowest tenderer and he got the contract at his price of 55 cents per cubic yard. Surely it is important, in considering the adoption of this resolution and the granting of this committee of inquiry to ascertain whether or not in this whole transaction, from the beginning to the end, there is anything reflecting upon the conduct of the Minister of Public Works,_ either the previous minister or myself since I have had charge of this department. I say, that so far as Mr. Hyman is concerned, there is not a particle of evidence and there is not even a suggestion that he swerved one iota from the duty which he was sworn to perform. What does my hon. friend ask? He asks that without a particle of evidence, wihout a charge, without even an insinuation so far as Mr. Hyman is concerned, a committee of this House should be solemnly



appointed in order to inquire as to whether or not Mr. Hyman did his duty as a Minister of Public Works. Sir, Mr. Hyman, is not here to answer for himself, but I would be sorry as one member of this House, to be a party to the appointing of a committee to investigate the conduct of a former minister of the Crown who is not now a member of parliament, without some member at least having ventured to make some suggestion against his conduct.
What about the present minister?

My hon. friend will hear about the present minister by and by. I am speaking now with regard to the late minister, because when this House is asked to appoint a committee to investigate the awarding of this dredging contract it is not to investigate any charge against me, but to investigate the conduct of a gentleman who formerly occupied the position which I have now the honour to fill, it is to investigate the conduct of Mr. Hyman when he was Minister of Public Works and I can appeal to those gentlemen who knew Mr. Hyman when he was Minister of Public Works, who knew how well he performed his duties as minister, to say whether some charge or some statement or some evidence or some fact should not be presented to this House before a committee should be appointed to inquire into his conduct as Minister of Public Works in connection with the awarding of this contract. There is, as I have said, no pretence upon the part of Mr. Mayes that he had any improper communication with Mr. Hyman, there is no pretence upon Mr Mayes' part that Mr. McAvity had any improper communication with Mr. Hyman; and, with the evidence, as I have said, all the one way, the evidence that tenders were invited in the ordinary public way by public advertisement, that the tenders were received in the ordinary way and that the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer, it does seem to me that so far as Mr. Hyman and his conduct in connection with the awarding of this contract are concerned, there is nothing to lead in any way to the suspicion that he did not act in an entirely proper manner and entirely in the public interests. Does my hon. friend suggest that Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes were informed of what the tender of Messrs. Haney & Miller was? Does he suggest that?
Not at all, not at all.
Very well, not at all. My hon. friend does not even insinuate that?
No reason to even suspect any such idea.

Very well, I am glad to hear my hon. friend say that. Then what does it come to? It comes to this: That my hon. friend admits that there was no collusion between Mr .McAvity and Mr. Mayes, and the minister.
I admit nothing more than I have stated.

My hon. friend must admit _ that Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes had no information as to what was the amount of the next tender, and that being so, they simply put in their tender at 55 cents per cubic yard, and they took their chance of that being the lowest tender. And, Mr. Speaker, the very fact that there was a difference of 45 cents per cubic yard between their tender, which was the lowest, and that of Messrs. Haney & Miller, which was next to them, is the very strongest evidence of the fact that there was no collusion. Then there was the other fact that the tender of Mr. Mayes on boulders was reduced by 30 cents per cubic yard as compared with what it was under the first tender, and that there was also a change made by Haney & Miller in the price they asked for boulders as well as in the price they were asking for ordinary material. But everything connected with the letting of the contract in the departmental records, and everything which Mr. Mayes has stated, is absolutely consistent with the fact that so far as the minister was concerned, and so far as the officials of the department were concerned, everything was regular and proper. And yet, Sir, we are asked undeT these circumstances to investigate the conduct of a former minister of the Crown in awarding this contract in a regular and proper manner to Mr. Mayes. Let me say this to my hon. friend, and I say it as a lawyer; I say it as one who has had very considerable experience-I have seen the question asked in the newpapers: ' Why does not the Crown proceed against Mr. McAvity? ' Let me say, Sir, that if the Crown could proceed against anybody it would not be against Mr. McAvity, but it would be against that bosom friend of the member for St. John, Mr. Gershon. S. Mayes.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker-
Order.

Because, Sir, it was to Mr. Gershon S. Mayes this money was paid. The Crown had no contract with Mr. George McAvity; the Crown paid no moneys to Mr. George McAvity, and the Crown would have no case and no claim of any kind or description against Mr. George McAvity. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) is solicitous for this inquiry in order to see whether the Crown has a claim.

Let me say to my hon. friend that if it is true, as he says, that Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity had no knowledge of what was the next tender; if it is true, as will appear from all the evidence and all the facts we have before us, that there was no collusion of any kind between Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes and the minister, and that there was no irregularity in the letting of the contract, let me say that the Crown could have no action against Mr. Gershon S. Mayes. The only ground upon which an action could be founded is that there was collusion. Suppose two people are about tendering for work with any department, and one of them says to his partner:
' Now, I control this matter and I am willing for myself to do this work at a certain figure/ and the other partner says: 'No, we can get more for that; I do not think there is anybody else in the country who will do it for the low figure at which you think of tendering, and we are perfectly safe in tendering at a larger figure/ and a tender is put in and it is dealt with in a proper manner, and upon the advice of the officers of the department that contract is awarded, and the Crown discovers afterwards that one of the partners who might have controlled it would have been quite willing to put in a tender for a smaller amount, could the Crown turn around and bring an action against the firm to recover back the money which it might have saved? Now, in the absence of collusion, that is exactly the case here. My hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) says that Mr. George McAvity became interested with Mr. Gershon S. Mayes in this contract, and if it had not been for Mr. George McAvity Mr. Mayes would have tendered for a lesser figure. But Mr. Mayes did not tender for a lesser figure, and he did not tell the minister that he was willing to do the work for a lesser sum.
He did tender and he could not get the contract.
My hon. friend need not have brought that in because it has no bearing on the point. He tendered some months before.
Exactly, for the same work.

That was under another call for tenders and at that time he had not a dredge and the contract could not be awarded to him, and so far as the Minister of Public Works could know he might have changed his mind a thousand times between June and September.	He might
have ascertained in the interim that the work was more difficult than he anticipated and the minister would know nothing about it. The point I make is, that his tender being put in in the regular way in response to a public call for tenders, his tender having been accepted by the minister in good faith, I care not how much he may have 137J	,	I	! i
paid Mr. George McAvity, the Crown has no claim against Mr. Gershon S. Mayes for one dollar of the money which was paid under that contract. And, my hon. friend might as well face it first as last, that the only ground upon which any claim could be made by the Crown against either Mr. McAvity or Mr. Mayes is that there was collusion between them and the department, that there was fraud upon the paTt of the late Minister of Public Works, that he conspired with these people to enable them to get the contract in fraud of the public and against the public interest. That is the only ground upon which a claim could be made, and if my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) wants this committee appointed, and if he wants to see whether this money can be recovered back, let him have the courage to say that the Hon. Charles S. Hyman, while a member of this House, and while Minister of Public Works, was guilty of this fraudulent act and that he was a party to this money having been taken from the public treasury-
Will the minister allow a question?
Sit down.
If I am out of order I will sit down.
I have no objection to the hon. gentleman asking his question.
Will the minister say whether in his opinion that was a legal contract between Mayes and McAvity.
I would not be at all adverse to giving an opinion to my hon. friend on that question if it were at all before the House, but that is a question between Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes.
And the minister too.
I would say this to my hon. friend, and I will not charge him any thing for this opinion-
That is a very unusual thing.
I would say to my hon. friend that I understand that Mr. Mayes has sued Mr. McAvity, and why? Because Mr. McAvity did not get any favours from the Department of Public Works.
Hear, hear.
If the minister would allow me I may say
Sit down.
I would consider that a good cause for action, because the understanding on which Mr. McAvity got into the agreement was that he would get favours.

And my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) has actually read to this House a letter-he has actually fathered this letter, too-in which Mr. Gershon S. Mayes complains of Mr. George McAvity that he has not succeeded in getting favours from the Department of Public Works. And that is the ground upon which, just a few days before the election, almost simultaneously with the reading of this affidavit-and let me say. Sir, that the people of St. John accepted it at its true worth, and let me say further, Mr. Speaker, the people of the whole province of New Brunswick accepted it at its true worth. While we had in that province a splendid cause to fight for, and while we had most acceptable candidates in every comity in the province, yet I am almost inclined to think that some small measure of the success which we achieved in that contest was owing to the unfair tactics of our opponents, was owing to their determination, shown day after day and week after week, to resort to all kinds of slander, to hesitate at nothing in order to achieve success, winding up with the reading, by the premier of the province, of this false affidavit, at the great Conservative meeting in the city of St. John.
At six o'clock the House took recess. After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the House rose at six o'clock, I had made the remark that perhaps the great success which the Liberal narty had won in the province of New Brunswick was to some extent-possibly only to a small extent-assisted by the conduct of the members of the Conservative party in that province, particularly the leader of that party and the present premier of New Brunswick in reading this affidavit at the great Conservative meeting held in St. John on the 12th of October. That was but the culmination of the attacks and of a course of action of a very discreditable character, which, it was hoped, would injure the Liberal cause in the province of New Brunswick, but which signally failed. True, my hon. friend from St. John, (Mr. Daniel) succeeded in getting ^ back to parliament, but he and his colleague who sits beside him (Mr. Crocket) represent all that is left of the once great Conservative party of that province. Of course, they did not spring this affidavit on the public until a comparatively short time before the election, but still where the people had the opportunity of studying the whole question, where they have known me a great many years-because I have lived among the people of St. John upwards of a quarter of a century -they gave a pretty emphatic verdict with regard to these attacks, so far as I myself was concerned. And so far as the hon.

gentleman who represents the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) is concerned, while he has succeeded in being elected, the Conservative majority of very nearly 1,000, wfiich he had in 1904, was cut down to 192. And the majority of about 600 which the late lamented Dr. Stockton had in 1904 was converted into a majority of nearly 6,500 for myself in the constituency which I represent. I have always been ready and willing to meet any attack made upon myself, and it has given me great pleasure to day to have the opportunity of meeting the insinuations which are contained in the statement presented to the House. What I always desire is that I shall meet my opponents in the open, that I shall have the opportunity of facing them, and I have never been afraid-and I trust never shall -to meet my enemies under any circumstances. My hon. friend who represents one of the constituencies of Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) asked the question before recess: What about the present Minister of Public WoTks? Well. I shall tell him, so far as this contract is concerned. But first let me ask him if he would join in the insinuations now being made in the Conservative press that I was in some way, directly or indirectly, connected with Mr. Mc-Avity in the advantages got from this dredging contract. If he, or any other hon. gentleman, would join in that suspicion or insinuation, let me ask him whether, if what they suspect were the case, he would not think it strange that I should have asked Mr. Mayes for money instead of going to Mr. McAvity, who, it appears, was to get considerable advantage out of this contract. Or does he not think, if if were understood that I was interested, directly or indirectly, that Mr. Mayes would have referred me to Mr. McAvity instead of giving me this $2,000 for services which he ays was not due me at all and to which I was in no way entitled. I desire to say-and I say it in the most emphatic Planner and in the strongest language possible-that I had no interest at any time, either in 1905 or any time since, directly or indirectly in that contract, that I was not benefited in any way directly or indirectly, by it, or in whatever was derived from it by Mr. McAvity. In 1905, I acted simpiy as the solicitor of Mr. Mayes and was discharging towards him the duty which I thought, as his counsel and solicitor, I might fairly perform. He came to me as his legal adviser, as one who had advised him during a great many years in many important matters, and he asked me if I could Tefer him to any business man in St. John who would be likely to engage with him in this dredging enterprise. I mentioned Mr. George McAvity as a man of means and large experience whom I thought it would be greatly to his advantage to have as a partner. It was under those circumstances, and for that rea-

son and no other, that I referred him to Mr. McAvity. What their arrangements or relations were I never knew, beyond having the general knowledge that they were interested together in the dredging contract, and I assumed that their relations were those of ordinary partners engaged in an ordinary business transaction.
If it is asked: What about my own conduct? I think I can fairly answer that the best way to judge is to look at the record and see whether or not I honestly and faithfully discharged the duty which I owe the public as Minister of Public Works. If any hon. gentleman can find in the correspondence any statement made by Mr. Mayes or anybody else that I ever showed towards him or Mr. McAvity, in connection with this contract, any favour or consideration which might not fairly be shown the veriest stranger, then an indictment might fairly be brought against me. But if I am able to point to the record and show that, although requests were made me from time to time to grant certain favours to Mr. Mayes, and although those requests were made both by Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes, I refused them in every instance and held Mr. Mayes strictly to the performance of the contract, and if I can show specially that there is strong evidence that neither had I any interest in the matter nor was I influenced by friendship towards either party, then I submit that all these insinuations fall to the ground.
I wish to refer again for a moment to the statement that in the interest of Mr. McAvity I held back moneys which were due to Mr. Mayes. I have given that statement an unqualified denial. It is said that he should have been given this money in the summer of 1908-in the month of August, if I remember well. I made inquiry from the deputy minister of my department with regard to the day when the final estimates were submitted, and I received this certificate from him:

cents still owing.

I will tell you why I held back that amount. I had given directions for the payment of the entire sum to Mr. Mayes. But when I went to St. John, I found that certain of the ships berths there which, under the arrangement between the government and the city Mr. Mayes had contracted to dredge out,-or, rather to sweep out, using the more correct expression-had not been
swept out. So far from his performing his contract, he had left a very considerable amount of sweeping undone, and it was reported to me that the big ships would not be able to berth there by reason of his not having performed his contract. Finding this to be the case, I at once telegraphed to the chief engineer-or had Mr. Scammell telegraph, I am not sure which-to hold back certain moneys until Mr. Mayes should perform his contract. I did this in the interest of the people of St. John. And, let me say if I had known at that time facts which have been disclosed since, I would have had more of the money coming to Mr. Mayes held back, because over upon the northern side of the Sand Point slip, in these ships' berths which he was supposed to have dredged, we have discovered a considerable number of boulders which it was Mr. Mayes' duty to remove, and which the department has been called upon since to remove at very considerable expense. Mr. Mayes received money to which, I am bound to say, I do not think he was fairly entitled. And if I had known what I know now, a further amount beyond the $5,000 would have been held back. I state definitely-and I defy contradiction; I defy my hon. friends opposite to look through the correspondence and find anything to contradict me-that I have never held back any money from Mr. Mayes to which he was entitled, and I have never delayed the payment, except, as I have said, in the case of the $5,000 held back by reason of his not having performed his contract for the work of which I have spoken.
Now, I wish to take up some correspondence which has already been published. I speak now only of matters of which I have personal knowledge. If I had not personal knowledge, I would not read from the copies contained in the newspapers, but I am aware they are correct, and my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) if he looks at the files, I have no doubt, will see the letters there. The first letter is dated November 23, 1907, after I had become Minister of Public Works. Mr. Mayes wrote me this letter:
St. John, November 23, 1997. Hon. Wm. Pugsley,
Minister of Publio Works, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Permit me to call your attention to the fact that I have not been paid for any work for the last three months. This is entirely due to the appropriation having been exhausted and does not reflect upon anybody. Notwithstanding this, at your request, I have prosecuted this work under my contract just as diligently as if I were receiving the money regularly.
I may say that it was necessary to go on with this work in order to get ready for the steamships expected in the then coming winter.
I am sure you can understand what a burden this has imposed upon me when you con-

tider the extreme difficulty of getting money fiom our banks for any purposes. I have a l-'rge overdraft for which I am paying a heavy rate of interest. Had I so chosen, I could under the terms of my contract have stopped work altogether and thereby practically stopped my expenses, but the result would have been that the work would not have been advanced to an extent necessary to provide for the opening of the winter port season, which it practically is to-day. Under these circumstances I would suggest that you should cancel my old contract from the date of the last payment under it and substitute a r.ew contract embodying all the work which remained unperformed at that date, together with the work since awarded to me and which has recently been surveyed by Messrs. Vali-quet and Holt, this work to be at the same schedule as paid to the Dominion Dredging Company for similar, though in many instances, not so difficult work as we have had, the section, which contains nearly all the boulders in that vicinity, entailing serious breakage and great expense and loss. Besides this, you will find upon inquiry, that before I entered upon my first contract a gieat portion of the high water work which belonged to it had been removed by the local government dredges. Consequently, ,1 have Byways had an undue proportion of low water ,w.hich has added very materially to the difficulties of my work.
Trusting that this request may receive your most favourable consideration.
I remain, yours sincerely,

This gentleman, whose affidavit is now presented to the House, is represented as being_ eager to take the contract at 50 cents a cubic yard. Yet his request is that, owing to the difficulties of the work, he should be allowed to cancel his old contract and be given a new contract at 90 cents per cubic yard, the rate which he was getting under a later contract awarded to him after public tender by the gentleman who was acting Minister of Public Works previous to my appointment. Mr. Mayes made out a strong case, but not strong enough to warrant me as I thought, in the public interest, in acceeding to his request. I wrote him this letter :
16th December, 1907.
Dear Sir,-I have had under careful consideration your letter of the 23rd ult., asking to he relieved of your contract of the 30th September, 1905

That is the contract in question.
-and after consulting with the chief engineer of my department and examining the contract and specifications very carefully, I have come to the conclusion that it will not be possible to comply with your request, and I have therefore to ask that you will proceed as rapidly as possible and complete the work required under said contract.

Then I find another communication relating to this matter-and I intend to read this in order to show you that I endeavoured to perform my duty to the public and was not in any way influenced in the manner which these gentlemen would have you, Mr. Speaker, believe I was influenced; that I did not, as they have intimated, use my position for the purpose of aiding and assisting Mr. McAvity. This is a telegram which came to me:
St. John, October 10, 1907.
Mayes defies me. In his work absolutely refuses to dredge in accordance with instructions given in writing and also personally

I replied by telegram as follows:
Ottawa, 12th October, 1907.
J. K. Soammell, C.E., St. John.
Your telegram received. Carry out instructions of chief engineer.

Which meant that he was to keep Mr. Mayes right down to the performance of his contract. Now, we come down to the spring of last year.
Hon. Dr. Pugsley, Ottawa, Ont.
My dredge ' Beaver ' has been working nearly three years without being registered. Is there a necessity for registering next week for tendering other works, prefer not to.

To which I replied on the 18th as follows
G. S. Mayes, St. John, N.B.
Same condition is in all advertisements issued calling for dredging tenders. Regret find it impossible to make exception in your case.
(Sgd.) WM. PUGSLEY.

This telegram relates to a new work entirely that I was about to undertake in 1908, and in respect of which the advertisement went out in the ordinary way, with the condition that the dredge should be registered in Canada. We have more dredges now than we had in 1905.
Will the minister read the answer he gave?

This is the answer:
G. S. Mayes:
Same condtion as in all advertisements issued calling for dredging tenders.
That is, all advertisements that my department is now issuing calling for tenders.
Regret, find it impossible to make exception in your case.

Hon. Wm. Pugsley,
Minister of Public Works.
Dear Dr. Pugsley,-I wired you yesterday, that my work was completed and now beg to confirm it by letter. It was rather surprising, therefore, when the removal of 3,000 yards completed the job. As it is very evident that another error has been made, perhaps you will be good enough to point out some 9,000'yards for me to do elsewhere.
