I remain,
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) G. S. MAYES.
And probably under this original contract, whatever work Mr. Mayes would get, Mr. McAvity would get a share of it, and if I wanted to aid Mr. McAvity as a friend, I would naturally be disposed to encourage Mr. Mayes in getting additional work, and consent to his request for additional work. Then he says:
If so, I am ready and willing to do the work.
P.S.-May I call your attention again to the very large amount of money in holdbacks on progress estimates which are now due to me on these accounts. Please have the payment made as soon as possible as I have use for funds.
That date is in July, 1908. On August 10 I received this telegram from Mr. Mayes:
Have kept crew on dredge awaiting possible word from you as to dredging Ballast wharf berths. It can be done more satisfactorily this time of year as place is badly exposed to fall
and winter weather, this now.
Can you kindly arrange G. S. MAYES.
To which I replied on the same date as follows:
Regret unable to comply with your request.
My reason being that when the time came for this work to be done, I intended to put it up to public competition, and was not disposed to let it to Mr. Mayes by private contract. Now in addition to the letters which I have read, there are other letters on file which my hon. friend has had an opportunity of examining, and in which Mr. Mayes was contending that he had a claim against the department because my inspector had not allowed him full measurements; he was making a claim also that he should be allowed $19.60 for the removal of boulders instead of something over $8 which his contract provided for, and his requests in all these particulars I refused and held him down firmly to his contract. Then when he began to feel that he was not going to be shown any favours by me, he writes intimating that he is going to appeal to other members of the government for that justice which I was denying him. Let me say here that the man who gives to Mr. Mayes, from my experience of him, what he thinks is justice, may possibly be doing an injustice to other interests which might be entrusted to his charge. At all events, I simply did what I thought was my duty, I refused to accede to Mr. Mayes' requests. Along in the summer of 1908 he made up his mind that he would like to get out of the dredging business, and he approached me to see if I would not buy his dredge for the Public Works Department, and the price which he wanted was $150,000, or thereabouts. He began to intimate to friends of mine that if I did not buy his dredge there would be some disclosures made which would be very injurious to the Liberal party. He did not expect, I think, that I would be influenced by any of his threats, or by any of his intimidations which he was making, but I think he hoped that by going to my friends and telling them, perhaps half the story, he might induce them to endeavour to bring some influence to bear upon me to purchase his dredge. Well, my department required a dredge, and I was willing to buy his dredge if I could get it at a fair and reasonable price. I desire to say here that word came to me from most reputable friends, and amongst others from Mr. C. J. Osman, who was formerly speaker of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick, a gentleman of the highest character, a man whose woTd would be taken more quickly than the affidavit of many people, and a gentleman whom I think my hon. friend from St. John also knows and esteems.

The Hon. Mr. Osman is a very respectable gentleman, formerly a member of the legislative assembly; I believe he was defeated at the last election. I have great regard foT him, as I have for Mr. Mayes.

Well, it happens, Mr. Speaker, that there is a difference between the two gentlemen. Mr. Osman has occupied a very high and responsible position in the province of New Brunswick; to-day he is manager of a great manufacturing enterprise in the parish of Hillsborough in the county, of Albert. He is a gentleman whose word will be taken everywhere in the province of New Brunswick as a man of the highest hotiour. He has been my friend for a good many years; and one day, during the time of the general election, he came to me in the city of St. John, in a state of considerable excitement, and he said to me that Mr. Mayes had seen him and shown him a photograph of a promissory note for $2,000 which he had given me, and I think also the photograph of the cheque which he had given in payment. He led Mr. Osman to believe, so Mr Osman told me, that he had given me that note at a time when I was Minister of Public Works. Mr. Osman was greatly disturbed about it, and thought that he would come to me as a friend and as a member of the party, and give me notice of what Mr. Mayes had said.
Did the note bear the date on its face?

Apparently Mr. Osman did not notice it if it was in the photograph. Mr. Osman did not tell me as to that, but he has said to me and has stated over his own signature that Mr. Mayes led him to believe it was given when I was Minister of Public Works. I said: ' Did he tell you when the note was given? ' He said: ' No.' I said: ' It was in 1905, when I was solicitor for Mr. Mayes,' and I told Mr. Osman he need not worry. Mr. Osman said he was glad to hear it and he returned to his home in Albert county. Mr. Mayes intimated to Mr. Osman that if he could get $150,000 for the dredge, good Conservative as Mr. Mayes was, and I judge still is, there would be, out of this price of $150,000, a contribution of $20,000 towards the Liberal campaign fund. Mr. Speaker, that statement was made not only to Mr. Osman, so Mr. Osman told me, but to several other people of great repute in the city of St. John who all had the same story to tell of these approaches which were made to them by Mr. Mayes, and to different people the threat was made that unless this dredge was bought and an arrangement made to settle these claims, some dreadful and damaging disclosures would be made. To Mr. F. W. Holt, as Mr. Holt has declared by a solemn declaration. Mr. Mayes showed all the documents and photographs and

said he was about proceeding to Fredericton to have them published in a newspaper with which my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) is familiar, viz : The Fredericton 'Gleaner,' and that they would be published before the election and of course go broadcast throughout the country and do great damage to the Liberal cause. It happened that Mr. Mayes did not succeed either by these intimations made to my friends or by influences of any other kind, in accomplishing his desires. Among others whom he had approached was Mr. John B. M Baxter, an alderman of St. John and then vice-president of the Liberal-Conservative Association, whom Mr. Mayes had got to interest himself in the hope of selling this dredge to my department. On the 30th day of September, 1908, Mr. Baxter sent me this telegram:
St. John, N.B., Sept. 30, 1908. Hon. Wm. Pugsley,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Client impatient at hot receiving word from you or inspector

And the client is Gershon S. Mayes-
Client impatient at not receiving word from you or inspector. Quotes your purchase and payment for dredge ' Industry ' by order in council

That is the dredge which the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has been inquiring about-and I wonder if he has been having communications from Mr. Mayes on the subject-
Quotes your purchase and payment for dredge ' Industry ' as sufficient precedent for buying his dredge with complete equipment, ready for instant work at smaller price. Points out that fund for purchase is not exhausted or arrangement could be made similar to British Columbia purchase.
Mr. Mayes keeps in touch with all the dredge purchases made.
Advise act immediately, and wire definitely as client insists on prompt decision.

In reply to Mr. Baxter's telegram the following letter was sent by myself:
St. John, N.B., Oct. 7, 1908.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your telegram of the 30tli ult. in regard to dredge ' Beaver ' which was recently examined by the general superintendent of dredging. I regret to say that his estimate of the value of the spares is very much less than the estimate given by Mr. Mayes; and upon his report it would be impossible for me to recommend the purchase of the dredge at the price Mr. Mayes puts upon it.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) WM. PUGSLEY.
Mr. Speaker, I have given you a part of the correspondence and I invite my hon. friends opposite, if there is any one who

ventures to believe or who would like this House to believe that I ever showed Mr. Mayes or Mr. McAvity any favour in connection with this dredging contract or that I ever deviated one hair's breadth from the line of my duty as Minister of Public Works, I call upon him to read it to this House, I call upon him to give to this House and to the country information which he has upon that point. I declare, Sir, that every letter, every telegram which passed between us, every departmental act of mine, every act of mine as Minister of Public Works, will show that I faithfully discharged my duty as between Mr. Mayes, the contractor, and the people of this country.
Now, Mr. Mayes, having tried first by suggestion that there would be a contribu-ton to the campaign fund, a suggestion which did not succeed, because I suppose we did not require any campaign fund

Hear, hear.
Mr. PUGSLEY -At all events. Sir, we did not require any campaign fund to be contributed to by Mr. Gershon S. Mayes, nor by anybody else in return for any favours to him or any one else having dealings with the government of this country. After he had failed to accomplish his object by these suggestions, after he had failed by an attempt at blackmail, and after he found that he could not dispose of his dredging plant to the government and could not get his claim settled except in the ordinary way, and get just what he was entitled to get, after he found too that he could not get his contract cancelled, and could not get me to engage to give him a larger amount than he was in justice and by law entitled to, what did he do? He then went to the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick and handed him this affidavit for the purpose of having it read at the great Conservative meeting in the city of St. John on the 12th of October. That meeting was attended by prominent Conservative statesmen from other parts of Canada, among whom was Sir James Whitney, the premier of the province of Ontario. I am told, Sir, and I believe it is just possible, that the reason why my hon. friend succeeded in saving his bacon in the election in St. John was that he and his friends repudiated all knowledge of this affidavit until after it was read; my hon. friend said that this was a great bombshell which Mr. Hazen had been keeping up his sleeve for the purpose of exploding that night, and he and his friends admitted that instead of being a bombshell it proved to be a veritable boomerang and did great damage to the Conservative party. As I said, Mr. Mayes handed to them this affidavit and they made the most of it before the elections. It did not do them any good then and I do not think the fathering
of it by my hon. friend and the reading of it in this House is going to do him and his party very much good now or in the future.
I fear I have already taken too much of the time of the House, but I felt it was necessary that I should refer to these matters in order that the members of the House and the people of the country generally might know just what are the facts of this case, so far as they have come under my own observation and so far as I am able to speak with regard to them.
I simply wish to say this, and I say it with a good deal of sorrow, Sir, that the tactics which were used in the city of St. John and which culminated in the reading of this affidavit were calculated to bring disgrace upon the public life of this country. There is nothing more discreditable, there is nothing more unworthy of those who aTe seeking the confidence of the people than that instead of trying to build themselves up on their own conduct and merits, they should seek to discredit and to destroy the reputation of their opponents by false statements and by slanders. But, Sir, my personal experience in the city of St. John was not very different from that experienced by others in other sections of the country. In the province of Quebec we found the name of Sir Lomer Gouin, the premier of that province, forged to a telegram designed to assist his opponents in the election. Out in the province of British Columbia, upon the eve of the election, when the public mind was excited upon the Asiatic question, when everything depended upon the attitude of the two great parties on that question, we found there a forged telegram read at a public meeting, which no doubt was intended to and designed to and which no doubt did have a most material effect upon the election in the city of Victoria. Down in my own constituency, a few days before the election when the people were in the midst of the excitement of a political contest, at this great Conservative meeting they sought to destroy my character and to injure the Liberal party by reading a false affidavit and publishing it broadcast in the newspapers of this Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Such were the tactics of the Conservative party, and I regret to have to say it. They sought to make me suffer by these disgraceful tactics, but. Sir, I am happy to say that the people of the province of New Brunswick viewed such conduct as it should be viewed, and they not only returned me as the representative of one of the most important constituencies in that province, but they sent back ten staunch Liberals with me to support the government. That is the best answer that can be made to the tactics which were used at that time, and which I may say are of a similar character to those which have

for a good many years been directed against me.
I want to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that while I have made mistakes, as every man who has been a long time in political life has made mistakes, they have been errors of the head and not of the heart. I have endeavoured at all times to do what I thought was in the public interest. While 1 was in the provincial arena I endeavoured to discharge my duty to the public, and when I received the very high honour of being called by the Eight Hon. the Prime Minister to take a seat in his cabinet, I made up my mind that I would be even more zealous than I ever was before foT the public weal. I have endeavoured at all times, Sir, to perform my duties, not only as a member of parliament, but as minister, in what I conceived to be the best interests of the country. And let me say that if there is any gentleman on the opposite side of the House-my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) included-who feels that there is any ground for an attack against me in reference to this contract, or any other, then I say the fair and manly course is to make a charge against me with regard to the administration of my department. And let me say also to these Conservative newspapers which are levelling their vile attacks upon me and seeking to injure my reputation and my character that it would be fair for them to appeal to seme gentleman upon the other side of the House to make a direct and specific charge against me so that I may know what I have to answer, so that an inquiry may take place, and so that witnesses may be called to the end and that we may know whether I am guilty or not guilty of those insinuations which are hurled against me. That, it seems to me, is the fair and manly course to take, and that, it seems to me, is but a small measure of the justice which every public man in this country is entitled to have meted out to him.

I am not going to read the correspondence which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works read this afternoon, but after reading that correspondence and after listening to it I ask again if his is the conduct of a guilty party.
Mr. Mayes came to Ottawa about a year ago or a little less. He came while the estimates were going through last May or June, and I am credibly informed that he carried this story to the Conservative party, and that a member of the Conservative party came to a gentleman who occupies a seat in this House from the province of Nova Scotia, and told him the story. That gentleman came to me, told me the story and he thought that there was something which might get some one into trouble. Mr. McAvity was telegraphed for, he came to Ottawa and Mr. McAvity said: You go back to your friend and you tell that friend to crack on the moment that he wants to. I think the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) knows who carried the story back. I can tell the hon. members of this House that nothing further was said about the Mayes business and that the estimates for dredging at St. John went through without opposition.
I might say to the hon. gentleman that I have not the most remote idea of what he is referring to.

I will accept the statement. Then we follow this down a little further. Mr. Mayes who was here last May or June, tried to get a renewal of his

contract. He commenced to blackmail the Minister of Public Works in August and he failed. Then the vice president of the Tory party in St. John went with an offer or a bribe of $20,000 for the Liberal campaign fund if they would buy his dredge. They would not buy it.
Is the non. gentleman not aware that Mr. Baxter, to whom, I presume, he refers, has denied that under oath?
Yes, and I am aware that a gentleman whom I would believe a great deal quicker says he did.
That seems to be a case for investigation then.
After everything had failed, after every device known to crooked men had failed
Oh, oh.

Mayes comes out with this affidavit. All I have to say about this Mayes affidavit is simply this:	A man
who, according to his own confession, will play the game that Mayes played in this matter from the beginning, a man who will play the hand that he played down a few weeks before the 12th of October would not hesitate to go further if he found it necessary, and draw an affidavit for the purpose of injuring the Minister of Public Works or of obtaining something which he thought might possibly help out his own personal ends. I am prepared, knowing the transaction and all the parties interested, to take the word of the Minister of Public Works against the whole bushel of affidavits made by a man like Mayes. When the Minister of Public Works tells this House that he had nothing to do with that contract, that he did not make anything out of it, there is nothing that I can see to investigate, and I would like to know why this thing has been brought up at this moment. There is no apparent reason for bringing it up. There are no great issues at Ottawa. There does not seem to be any reason on the surface why this matter should be launched at this particular time and two or three days of the valuable time of parliament taken up discussing it. But there is a reason beneath the surface, and I can tell you what it is. This was brought to the front for the first time last October when the Tory party were in dire distress, and again it is brought up in this month of April when that party are again among the breakers down in New Brunswick. I am prepared to say that it would be possible to have that party out of power in twenty-four hours by a rebellion among their own supporters in the New Brunswick legisla-Mr. CARVELL.
ture; and consequently this matter is now revived, not for the benefit of the people of the Dominion as a whole, but for consumption in the province of New Brunswick, in the hopes of diverting the attention of the people of that province from the troubles they are now having with their own local administration. That administration which was elected a year ago, with the support of over two-thirds of the representatives in the House of Assembly, that government which has since violated every pledge it ever made, either to friend or foe, which has only gone to the polls twice in the last year and got a black eye each time, which dares not open a constituency in that province to-day, whose supporters are seething in rebellion, and which feels bound to do something in order to draw awav public attention from its own sins, has taken this course, and imagines it will achieve its object by trying to blacken the fair fame of the Minister of Public Works. A similar attempt failed in October, 1908, but I am bound to say that, in my judgment, the present member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) occupies a seat in this House as a result of this false affidavit of Mayes. I cannot, therefore, agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that this affidavit did no harm to the Liberal party. It did do some hurt in many parts of the province of New Brunswick. I was some thirty miles out in the country the morning after ithe affidavit was read, and I was telephoned to come into town to meet my executive committee, and was told that if this thing were true I would have to denounce the whole matter or they would abandon me. I telegraphed the Minister of Public Works immediately and got back an answer, and when the afternoon papers came out, my people believed his reply, and I lost nothing by this affidavit. But I went to the city of St. John and I had occasion, after nomination day, to make a pilgrimage to the town of Sussex. I referred to this question there, and on my way back next morning,. I met a clergyman-a gentleman who occupied tne high position of president in the Methodist conference-and he told me that the ministerial association of the city of St. John had held a meeting the day before, and had decided that they could not vote for the government because of the revelations made in that affidavit.
I thought the hon. gentleman said there was nothing in it.

It was a whole tissue of falsehoods. That man told me that he believed Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right and the people needed his services another term, but in the face of that affidavit, he

could not vote for the government candidate and would not do it, and I assumed there were sufficient people in the city of St. John of the same mind as this clergyman to give my hon. friend the seat he occupies.
I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion there is no charge laid against the Minister of Public Works which requires investigation. If there be any hon. gentleman opposite who believes the statements in this affidavit-there seem to be two of them who do-let him get up like a man and make his charge. If any one will do that I shall hold up both hands to give the committee of investigation asked for, and I believe that every member on this side will do the same; and I have no doubt that Mr. McAvity will be the first man in New Brunswick who will welcome the opportunity to come here and tell what he knows about the transaction. Let these men come out in the open, and not remain under cover of a false affidavit, and let them, on their own responsibility, make their statement and they will have no trouble in getting an investigation.

NORLTHRUP, (East Hastings). I trust that I shall be able to avoid following in the footsteps of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr Carvell) and of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), who addressed the House at such length to-day, and confine myself to the subject before the House. I am encouraged to do so by the fact that it is perfectly evident that some gentlemen who have spoken on this resolution have not taken the trouble, Mr. Speaker, to read the amendment which has been put in your hands. And consequently we have lost half a day listening to very interesting historical disquisitions and to the whys and wherefores of many pregnant matters to the total neglect of the particular subject before the House. I trust that I shall be able to discuss this matter dispassionately, without saying a word to hurt the feelings of any hon. gentleman opposite, for, as I understand the question-and I think that other hon. members, on a moment's consideration, will take the same view-there is no necessity for the hard feeling and excited language given vent to so frequently to-day, and which have been aroused mainly by the fact that the Minister of Public Works has been so absorbed in some imaginary attack on himself and some of his friends that he has not had time to read the amendment. My hon. friend who last spoke (Mr. Carvell) after declaiming against the affidavit in question as a tissue of falsehoods, as absurd and inconsequential, wound up by telling us that in his own province the feelings excited were so great that people there, from clergymen down, were unwilling to support their old love, the Laurier government, if the statements in this affidavit were true. And we on this side, wishing to see the will of the people carried out, challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to give us the opportunity to find out whether or not this affidavit be true. I believe the Minister of Public Works to be too good a lawyer and too old and experienced a politician to have imagined for one moment, either this afternoon or any other time, that there was any attack made on him in this amendment.
What is the case before the House? This House is not a fit body to try whether or not certain statements are true. From what we have witnessed to-day, this House is preeminently unfitted to occupy a judicial position and decide whether or not certain charges made against a minister of the Crown, or his late colleague, are true or not, and this amendment does not ask the House to try this question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

It sets forth a certain momentous series of statements, and I venture to say that even the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Carvell) would not contradict the statement that if Mr. Mayes' affidavit be true-and it is not for me or any member on this side to say [DOT]it is-then the right hon. gentleman who leads the House owes it to himself to see that an investigation is made into its allegations. If that affidavit be untrue, then the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) is one of the most deeply wronged men in this country, and the man who does him the most wrong is the right hon. gentleman who refuses to give him an investigation in order that he may clear his reputation. It is unfortunate, perhaps, that we do not agree as to just what the nature of the charge is. Let me illustrate one point: The Minister of Public Works has taken a great deal of the time of the House to-day and on other occasions to dwell upon what he would have us believe to be a momentous error made in the original declaration. '1907, appearing instead of '1905.' I have read the affidavit very carefully, and I have listened to the statements made by the Minister of Public Works; and I venture to say that there is not one lawyer in Canada -not one lawyer in Canada-even the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) himself, who would not say that, in relation to the question before the House, it was a matter of utter indifference whether that declaration said '1907' or '1905.' And I will tell the minister why: There are two explanations of certain facts. Mr. Mayes gives one statement and the minister gives the other. And which ever you accept the result is the same, so that it is immaterial

whether that declaration related to 1905 or 1907. If the Minister of Public Works has stated . the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and if the $2,000 he received was in payment of legitimate legal costs, he had just as much right to receive those costs after he became Minister of Public Works as before. If, on the other hand, what Mr. Mayes swore is true, and if that $2,000 was paid for the assistance, the influence of the Attorne'' General of New Brunswick to be used in Ottawa to secure undue favours for this contractor, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) had no more right to receive that $2,000 before he was minister than afterwards. Why, the law read this afternoon, the Criminal Code of this country, places it beyond peradven-ture that if Mr. Mayes' story is true the Attorney General of New Brunswick, though not a member of this House then, was taking part in a transaction which is contrary to the law and the parties to which are liable to seven years in the penitentiary. Now, I wonder if there are not enough facts in this case for hon. members on either side who wish to do what is right, and who wish to know what the facts are, to agree upon and dispose of the question. I suppose we can start with the indisputable fact that Mr. Mayes was a client of the Attorney General of New Brunswick, and that they had conversations, and that Mr. McAvity was acquainted with the Attorney General of New Brunswick, and that he was the head centre for the city of St. John of the Liberal party, and that Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity had conversations about getting a contract in Ottawa. And I suppose that there is no dispute, as the Minister of Public Works allows, that Mr. Mayes had tried_ to get a contract at 49 cents for a certain kind of dredging. And there is no dispute that Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes came to Ottawa, and that they came to see about a contract, after a conversation between Mr. Mayes and the Attorney General of New Brunswick. There is no dispute that Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity came to the office of the then Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman), that Mr. Mayes remained outside and that Mr. McAvity went in. What took place within that room, I do not pretend to say. But so far, I think everybody will agree as to the facts. Up to the time that Mr. McAvity went into this office, Mr. Mayes had no contract, and, apparently, could not get one. Mr. McAvity came out and Mr. Mayes went in and got the contract at six cents more than he had tendered.

It does not state that. What the affidavit says is that Mr. Mayes went in and spoke to Mr. Hyman and asked him if he could get the contract for 400,000 yards, as he wanted to know that prior to bringing in his plant. And Mr. Hvman Mr. NORTHRUP.
said he would get it if he were the lowest tenderer.
What does the minister complain of in my statement?
The hon. gentleman said that the contract was closed then.

No, I said that Mr. McAvity went in, leaving Mr. Mayes outside. After a time, Mr. McAvity came out and Mr. Mayes went in. We do not know what took place, but we do know the fact that Mr. Mayes got the contract at six cents more than he had been trying to get it for months. And that very same day, or the following day-I think the same day a letter was written by the chief engineer of the department, promising Mr. Mayes 400,000 yards more. Now if Mr. Mayes got a contract for an additional 400,000 yards, I think the minister will admit that that contract was not given after public competition. We have no evidence as to the amount of advertising. I do not know about it, nor do I care; it is not material. Mr. Mayes got a certain contract which he had been trying to get, and, after a conversation with Mr. Hyman he got that contract increased by 400,000 yards.
That is not the evidence at all. It does not say that the 400,000 yards was additional.
It was not 400,000 yards originally. The amount was greatly increased.
The other tenders would cover 400,000 yards.

He was to have a guarantee of 400,000 yards, and the fact that a letter was written by Mr. Lafleur to that effect showed that it had not been closed in the first place. And then he went to get the dredge. And the very day he heard that his contract would be so much better even than the one he had tried to get and failed, Mr. Mayes signs an agreement to give Mr. McAvity all he got out of the contract over and above 50 cents. These are the facts. What did Mr. McAvity do for the difference between 50 cents and the contract price? That is one matter we want to have investigated. Nobody on either side has made the suggestion as to anything that Mr. McAvity did except to use his influence. Perhaps he did, perhaps he did not. But surely when a man gets a contract at six cents a yard more than he was willing to take the work for, and gets a much larger quantity of work than he had hoped, and when in getting it he was assisted by the head of the Reform party in his city, and when, immediately after, he makes the

agreement under which he is to pay $36,000 out of his contract, surely the subject is one for investigation. It is not for me to say Mr. McAvity did anything wrong.
I am not concerned about that. It is not for me to say Mr. Mayes is a saint; I know nothing of Mr. Mayes. But it is the duty of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who is responsible for the honour of parliament and of the proper conduct of the various departments, and who is responsible to the people of this country to whom he owes so much and who have trusted him so often, to see that their interest is protected, which interest, evidently, has not been protected when Mr. McAvity was getting out of such a transaction as this the sum of $36,000. One need mot go further than this far with the admitted facts to show that there is sufficient ground for an investigation. But there is another fact. The Attorney General of New Brunswick was paid $2,000 by this very man Mr. Mayes. It is not for me to say whether it was paid for the influence of this gentleman in obtaining the contract or in payment of legal costs. But when a man pledges his oath, thereby running the risk of going behind the prison bars if he has told an untruth, and declares that this payment of $2,000 was practically a rake-off for the Attorney General for his province in connection with getting a contract, I am not bound to believe it, but I am entitled to say to the right hon. gentleman who leads the House: Surely, Sir, this is a matteT for investigation. It is all very well for the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) who has just taken his seat to say in the most theatrical way that he has such confidence in the Minister of Public Works that he would accept his word against a bushel of affidavits. That very statement perhaps shows the utteT unfitness of this House as a judicial bench to try a question of this kind. Now it is perfectly certain, too, that after Mayes had finished his contract he was not immediately paid, there is no doubt about that. There may be a difference of opinion as to why he was not paid. Mr. Mayes may give one reason, and the Minister of Public Works may give another Teason why he was not paid, but the stubborn fact remains that he was not paid promptly after he had finished his contract.
He was paid in the ordinary course.

Surely in the face of this letter of the 22nd of August protesting against holding him up, the letter which was answered by the minister on the 24th of August, surely in the face of that correspondence the minister will not say that he was paid promptly. Just imagine the moral obliquity of Mr. Mayes if, when he
had been paid promptly for the work which he had finished in July, he should write on the 22nd of August such a letter as this:
Hon. Wm. Pugsley, Esq.,
Minister of Public Works, St'. John.
Dear sir

I regret that you have seen fit to withold from me the payment of my July estimates and the balance of my contract in consequence, as you state to me, of Mr. Geo. McAvity having wired you that I owed him a sum of money.
Now he was held up, and held up by Mr. McAvity, the gentleman who, he said, had been holding him up all along:
I do not think this is a consistent position for you to take. Mr. McAvity's bills against me are a personal matter, and are different entirely from anything between the government and myself. I consider that I have overpaid Mr. McAvity to a very large amount. He proposed to have certain conditions carried out by which I would obtain more dredging work, and would receive fairer and more equitable treatment from the officials of the department. He has utterly failed in this.
And the agreement under which he was to do that was executed on the 6th of September after he got his $400,000. and before he got his $36,000 for what he had done. Now, Mr. Mayes says he has not done any more for him. and so the rogues fall out-no, I do not wish to use hard terms-but these gentlemen fell out.
He has utterly failed in this, and I propose now to enforce my rights by bringing suit against him to recover the very large amount which I have paid him, some $36,000. You ai e perfectly aware that Mr. Mc/Vvity's claims against me is for percentages of my contracts n ith your department in consideration of his services in helping me to get a contract, and his promise that he would do all in his power to assist me to get others.
This is his opinion of the minister on the 22nd of August:
Knowing this as you do, I cannot understand why you should use your position to hold up the man who has earned the money that a middleman may exact his satisfaction.
Now I would like to ask the minister
Read my reply.
I will with pleasure, if you will send it over to me.
It has gone into the ' Hansard ' office. I will send for it.

I will read it if the minister gives it to me at any time before I resume my seat. But the point I wish to make clear is this, that Mr. Mayes, on the 22nd of August told the minister that he, Mr. Mayes, and Mr. McAvity had made a criminal contract under the statute law of this land, that McAvity was given his I percentages in violation of the very clauses

read by the hon. member for St. John. He wrote to the minister saying: You know this is the case, you knew it on the 22nd of August. And here the minister is being told by the contractor in the most remonstrating tone, I am surprised at you holding me up, I, the man who did the work, you, who know all the facts, that McAvity was only being paid to use his influence later, and you are holding me up and letting the middleman have the money and letting the man who did the work go without it. We will see, when we get the answer of the minister, what he said to this charge that he had known before of this state of affairs, and if he did not know it before, he knew it on the 22nd of August, and then the minister writes a letter in a jaunty tone saying: This is a matter of indifference to me. One would think that the minister who was guarding the treasury, when he found this statement made by the contractor, Mr. Mayes, would have felt himself entitled to bring an action against Mayes and McAvity for collusion, I would like to ask the Minister of Justice, if he were here, if the Crown had brought an action against Mayes and McAvity, and put McAvity in the witness box with that sworn declaration, what the verdict of a court would be in that case. We know what McAvity himself swore to, and it would be interesting to see the explanation McAvity would give, a gentleman whom I am not attacking, but who is lauded to the skies by the hon. member for Carleton, N. B. (Mr. Carvell); I would like to hear what his explanation of the reason by which he raked in $36,000 when, according to Mr. Mayes, he had done not one single thing, invested not one solitary dollar, and had merely used his influence with the minister to obtain a contract. Now that contract was an honest and proper contract or it was not. It is not for me to say whether it was one or the other, that is a subject for investigation. But if that was an honest contract, don't vou think, Mr. Prime Minister, that McAvity obtained the money under false pretenses, when he represented to Mayes: This is such a dishonest government that you will have to have my influence to get you an honest contract. And if it was an improper contract, don't you think Mr. Prime Minister,
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman should address the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order is properly taken.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the speaker, then, to ask the right hon. gentleman who leads this House what he thinks about these statements, whether he thinks that was an honest and proper contract that was made with Mr. Mayes or not, and if it was Mr. NORTHRUP
an honest and proper contract, one that any body might reasonably obtain, then I ask you to inquire of the right hon. leader of the House why McAvity got $36,000 out of it. Would it not strike an ordinary person that he must have obtained that money under false pretenses? And if it was an improper contract, then I think the right hon. gentleman owes it to himself and his party to see that there is an investigation to show how such a contract came to be made. Now here is the letter of the minister dated the 24th of August, which is a reply to the letter I have just read of the 22nd of August:

Mayes, St. John.
I am in receipt of yours of the 22nd instant, and in reply would remind you that when I informed you of the notice which I had received from Mr. McAvity that he was interested in the moneys coming to you from my department and had requested me not to pay them over until the matter was adjusted, you admitted that there was an amount coming to him, which you said you were prepared to pay, provided I would allow a further claim which you said you proposed making, and would buy your dredge. The impropriety of ycur proposal, which I told you I could not possibly entertain, did not seem to impress vcu as it ought to have done.
As you in your letter deny any indebtedness to Mr. McAvity, I do not propose to intervene in the matter, and shall give instructions for the payment to you of the amount found to he due you by the accountant of my department. If you have any further claim on the department, it will he dealt with on its merits. Y hether or not you owe Mr. McAvity or have overpaid him, or whether or not there should be litigation between you, is, I beg to assure }cu, a matter of perfect indifference to me.
That letter is in answer to the letter of the 22nd August, in which Mr. Mayes told the minister that a corrupt arrangement had been made between McAvity and himself. How long before, we do not know. Some people might think that that was corroborative evidence of Mayes' affidavit, that the Attorney General, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) knew of it from the beginning. But as the minister did not deny the statement in Mr. Mayes' letter, that he knew of it prior to being told by Mayes on the 22nd August, I think the right hon. the Prime Minister should consider that as a proper subject of investigation to find out when the minister first learned of this transaction. The matters to which I have referred so far are not in dispute between the various parties and the only question seems to be, when an affidavit is laid on the table of parliament setting forth these serious charges, what should parliament do? Parliament must do one of two things, either declare that these charges, solemnly sworn to, are of such trifling importance that we will decline even to investigate them, or else allow an investigation to be made. I do not

for a moment wish to dispute the word of the Minister of Public Works when he says there is not a word1 of truth in this, that or the other charge. I would be doing very wrong if I did question his word, particularly in view of the way in which the presentment of this case strikes me. I think it will strike every hon. member that nothing could be much more absurd than that, when charges are made, charges which the right hon. gentleman himself will admit, if true, will lead to some very serious results after investigation, it should be held to be a sufficient and complete answer to this House and to the people of this country, a sufficient vindication of the honour of the government, for the Prime Minister to say, as he may be assumed to say by the words of the last speaker:	'I
place more confidence in the word of the Minister of Public Works than in a bushel of affidavits and therefore I shall allow no investigation.'
We have to remember that matters such as this strike different people in different ways. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works perused an article in 'The Globe,' Toronto, a paper by no means hostile to himself. The editor of that paper, and it will not be said that he was animated by Conservative sympathy, out of the fulness of his heart poured out his regrets, almost his maledictions, on the Conservative party because they had driven out the Minister of Public Works who would have to return to his lucrative practice in St. John until after the matter was investigated, and charges similar to these cleared up. The article is a long one and I shall read only the concluding paragraph. It reads:
Mr. Pugsley's enemies will thus succeed in depriving the country
That has nothing to do with this.
That has no reference whatever to the Mayes matter.
Certainly, I am
That is entirely irrelevant to this. .

The charge made in the other case is different from this. I have not said that this charge is true, I have not said that the charge which the 'Globe' referred to is true, but I am endeavouring to show that such charges produce an effect on the public mind and that the only way to meet such an effect is to have an investigation.
We have precedents in the mother land, to which the Prime Minister is so fond of referring, that shed a light on the standard of public life in that country. Many members will remember the case of Lord Henry Lennox in 1876. Lord Lennox was then a member of the Conservative administration and he was also a director of the Lisbon tramways, an unfortunate company which had as a promoter a man who made improper promises and led certain shareholders to grief. One of the shareholders sued the promoter and the judges in giving judgment against the promoter said that the directors of the company must have neglected their duty or the company would not have found itself in such a condition Lord Henry Lennox was a director of the company, and also a minister of the Crown. These events had taken place five years before and I think that .. rd Lennox was not at that time a minister, as I do not believe a Conservative administration was then in power. A gentleman on the opposite side of the House dropped a line to Disraeli, the premier, to say that he intended to give notice of a question asking the government practically what they proposed to do in view of the utterance of the judges in the case, to which be it remembered, Lord Lennox was not a party at all, so that any remark of the judges was obiter dictum; yet as soon as this letter was sent to the premier he sent it to Lord Lennox, who at once tendered his resignation to the nremier; the following day ip the House Lord Lennox gave his explanation, and the premier followed saying that it was a painful thing to him to have received and accepted the resignation, but he pTaised the honour of Lord Lennox, who insisted on defending his own personal honour without the responsibility of office and without asking his colleagues to share the responsibility with him.
There was another case in the old country in 1903 when a Mr. Fisher was a member, I think, of the Conservative administration. Mr. Fisher was engaged with certain other gentlemen with regard to a patent. Matters went wrong and the undertaking was not a profitable one, but Mr. Fisher personally had no more to do with the matter that went wrong than you. Mr. Speaker, or I. But in the course of litigation it was evident that certain people who had taken stock were going to lose and it was suggested to Mr. Fisher that as some of these people might have taken stock relying on his name as a minister being connected with the company, it was his duty to see that they did not lose. Mr. Fisher paid them 20 shillings on the pound and resigned his seat in the House in order that no blame might rest on his colleagues, no matter how innocent he might be. Mr. Balfour spoke with regret at the unfortunate result of the disclosures, and spoke of Mr. Fisher's resignation as a loss to the country. Mr. Campbell-Bannerman spoke to the same effect, and a gentleman whose voice has often resounded through this House, the Hon. Edward Blake, could not allow the matter to pass without a few graceful words. He said:

What has happened to-day, however painful it may be to the hon. gentleman himself, has vindicated his own reputation

And here, Sir, is the point to which I wish to call the attention of the right hon. gentleman:
-and also maintained the honour and standing of this House.
It is as a member of this House, it is as a Canadian, that I appeal to the right hon. gentleman to allow this amendment to pass, to allow an investigation to be held, and, Sir, if an investigation is held, and it is found that this affidavit is untrue, that this man Mayes has been maliciously endeavouring to blast the reputation of a man who in that case would be far better than himself, the right hon. gentleman and his followers need not have the slightest fear that we on this side will do anything to save him from well-merited punishment, and if, on the other hand, the investigation should show that there is some foundation for his charges, then this House, having a report from a committee which had heard the evidence, which had placed Mr. Mc-Avity on oath and had heard from him personally and not through his representative, for the time-being, in the House, then parliament would be able to vote what should be done by way of commendation or punishment of the gentlemen really concerned.
It seems to have been lost sight of in this discussion that if Mayes' story be true, then of course the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) would be implicated in the latter part of the charge, with reference to holding up the payment until Mc-Avity was settled with. If that were not true and the first part were true, if it were true that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) had received $2,000 for the use of his influence in Ottawa, it would not be a matter so directly concerning this House. The hon. gentleman says: Let a member make a charge and I will welcome investigation. I wish the Minister of Justice was here in order that I might ask him on what ground any gentleman on this side of the House should stake his reputation and his seat in order to punish a man for what, he did before he_ became a member of this House, for which we could not punish him even if the facts stated in Mayes' affidavit were proved to be true right up to the hilt. Nobody would pretend to say, that if it were true-and I guard myself again by saying that I do not express an opinion myself-but if it be true that the then Attorney General of New Brunswick was paid $2,000 for his political influence at a time when he was not a member of this House, it would be idle for any one to pretend to say he had forfeited his seat in this House because of something he had done some years before he became a member. And while both sides will accept that pro-Mr. NORTHRUP.
position, it is another matter altogether, if it can be proven to be true, whether the Prime Minister would allow one of the most important posts in his administration to be held by a gentleman who had such a conception of his duty as a public man. This is so serious a matter that in the interests of the country we are entitled to have an investigation so that the truth may be declared one way or the other. I have tried to discuss the question without using any harsh language against any one. I think it is a simple question as to whether or not enough has been shown in this affidavit of Mayes, if true, to justify an investigation. We cannot here try whether or not it is true., but we can appoint a committee to try that question. And surely, it must be evident to every one that if Mayes' character is so bad and his reputation so shaky and his affidavit so worthless as has been said by gentlemen opposite, surely the biggest mystery in Canadian political life today is that the Minister of Public Works would not welcome an inquiry to roll aside the cloud. One other point and I am done. If the affidavit of Mayes be true, then there was the very collusion that the Minister of Public Works has spoken of, and if there was collusion-apart altogether from the question of conspiracy which has been dealt with by my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket)-if there was collusion, then without doubt McAvity is liable to hand back the $36,000 which he got for doing nothing.
Mayes does not say there was collusion with the Minister of Public Works.
Mayes tells his story.
He does not say there was collusion with Mr. Hyman.

He did not pretend to say there was collusion because he was not present, but if the facts set forth by Mayes are true, I do not think any judge or jury in the land would have any difficulty in finding there was collusion.
The member for York does not concur in that statement.

I frankly admit that I differ from the law as laid down by my hon. friend from York. I do not think it would be possible to have an investigation of this matter without the standing of the Minister of Public Works of that day being concerned. And certainly the standing of the Minister of Public Works of to-day would be concerned, first as Minister of Public Works if the charge as to the payment to McAvity were held to be true, and secondly, if the other charge of receiving $2,000 for his influence were true. I do think that the right hon. the Prime Minister is practically concerned in this matter, because he being responsible to

the people of this country for his ministers, it is his duty when a prima facie case is made-and nobody would deny that there is a prima facie case when a man makes an affidavit with all the surrounding evidence to corroborate that affidavit that we have here-surely it is a duty that the right hon. gentleman owes to himself to see that his departments of government are kept pure and clean. I sincerely trust, from the national' standpoint, from a Canadian standpoint, from the standpoint of a member of this House, that the Tight hon. gentleman will allow an investigation. I am sure the right hon. gentleman will believe me, I am sure eyery member in this honourable House will believe me when I say, that if I were not speaking for the interests of the country and of the House; if I were speaking merely as a Conservative partisan I should hope from the bottom of my heart that an investigation would be refused.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make the promise to the House that was made by the hon. member (Mr. Northrup) and that is, that I shall endeavour to stay with the question before the House, although I sincerely hope that I shall have more success in keeping that promise than he had. The hon. member began in what he seemed to oonsider was a very judicial frame of mind, and, he rebuked thq member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) for not keeping to the question before the House, but to my very great surprise the hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) very soon showed considerable partisanship in charging the hon. member for Carleton with a theatrical manner in the delivery of his speech. Without being an absolute authority upon the meaning of that adjective, I could not help thinking that the hon. member for Carleton probably owed .the favour of having that epithet hurled at him to the fact, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) thought he was usurping a function that is not altogether foreign to the manner of the member for Hastings himself. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) told us that in his opinion this House was not a fit tribunal to consider this question, but he immediately proceeded to give evidence that he thought there was in his own person at least one exception to that general rule, because in his speech he himself made a very exhaustive examination of the case. In the course of his speech the very strongest partisan attitude was taken by the hon. member (Mr. Northrup) himself, because he quoted the affidavit and all that Mr. Mayes says in the affidavit, against the word of the Minister of Public Works which we heard reiterated again and again with the most ample evidence to bupport it, in the
speech which the hon minister delivered in his defence to-day. I could not help wondering that the hon. member (Mr. Northrup) should have said that he could dispute the word of the minister, almost in the same breath in which he quoted the details of Mr. Mayes' affidavit against the word of the minister. One word more in regard to the member for Hastings will enable me to fulfil my promise to stay with the question. I must say that the honourable member was extremely unfortunate in the old country precedents which he cited to endeavour to prove his arguments. In the first place, the offence charged against the ministers in the old country was alleged to have occurred while they were ministers of the Crown and members of the House. That is not the present case at all. In the second place the ministers in the old country who were charged practically admitted the truth of the charge by at once resigning their positions. But in this case we have a diametrically opposite situation. We have the minister not only denying the charge which is brought against him but giving the most ample evidence that it is possible to give that the charges are foundationless. I would like to say that in my judgment this House is acting well with an undoubted right in having brought before it a resolution asking for a committee of investigation. It would be acting within its right to grant that committee, but I take it that the possession of a right is one thing and the light, frivolous or thoughtless exercise of that right is another thing.
All things are lawful, but all things are not expedient.
I do not recognize the relevance of the interruption of the hon. member.
I did not suppose you would.

In fact I think I would be getting within the toils of rule 19 by saying that my hon. friend is as irrelevant as he frequently is. I was saying that it is not always wise to exercise a right, and I take it that the very strength of this right of investigation on the part of parliament, is that parliament, whether in this country or in the old country, has recognized that the demand for such a committee and for such an inquiry is so very serious a thing that it should not be acceded to except upon the very strongest case that can be presented to parliament. I would like to say, Sir, that the appointment of a parliamentary commission for inquiry into the conduct of a member of the House, who is also a minister of the Crown, is not an ordinary expedient to be lightly undertaken. It is an extraordinary

expedient, only justified by a very strong case. What is the fact, Sir, that relates to_ the ordinary procedure of this House with regard to every member of it? We have had it stated again and again in the last week and it is that in the ordinary procedure of this House when a member, not a minister, but a member, rises in his place and makes a statement as to a fact, we accept that statement as true. Yet this commission is proposed to investigate a statement of the utmost detail, made with the very greatest ability and supported by evidence drawn fully from the correspondence in this case. In regard to the basis upon which it is proposed to build this commission, the man Mayes leaves upon my _ mind two very distinct impressions. I differ from my hon. friend from Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) in that I am not from New Brunswick, and anything I know about this case I have learned to-day. I have listened with as much. care and as much impartiality as I am capable of to the charges on the one hand and to the Teply of the minister on the other, and I have gathered two very distinct impressions about this man Mayes. The first one which I have does not depend upon the unsupported statement of the minister, but it came out clearly in the correspondence which he read and which he had had with this man. The first impression I gathered about him, founded upon the minister's statement and supported by the correspondence, is that he is a disgruntled seeker of government favours. I take it that that was clearly brought out by his correspondence with the minister. He wanted a higher price for a dredge than that dredge was worth. The minister refused that higher price, and doubtless the man who wanted to sell the dredge did not feel quite so well pleased as if he had been met by an agreement instead of a refusal. We have heard something in this debate about the minister holding up Mr. Mayes. Why, it seems that the boot is entirely upon the other leg. It was Mr. Mayes who unsuccessfully attempted to hold up the minister. I take it that that fact was brought out in the debate, and brought out by the correspondence without any possibility of dispute on the part of any fair-minded man amongst my opponents in this House, and I take it that that fact justified my first impression and justifies me in describing Mayes as a disgruntled seeker of government favours. The second fact about this man is that, by mistake or otherwise, he promulgated a false affidavit. I do not think that any member of the opposition benches will be able to deny the truth of that statement. He promulgated a false affidavit. He was either so careless about it that he got the wrong date inadvertently or he was so wicked about it that he got Mr. M. CLARK.
it on purpose. My hon. friends opposite may take which ever horn of a not altogether pleasant dilemma that suits them best, but I take it that the fact is clear that he promulgated a false affidavit. He proved the falsity of the affidavit by correcting it himself. On the strength of a corrected affidavit this House is asked to throw over the circumstantial and complete statement of a minister of the Crown and to appoint a commission of investigation. To investigate what? To investigate a case hanging upon, depending for its sole foundation upon the statement of a corrected affidavit by a disgruntled seeker of government favours, who admits that in the first instance he promulgated a falsehood. I do not know what the opposition may think about this way of putting the case. That is how it strikes a plain man from the west, and I must say that in my humble judgment there are very grave and very strong reasons why we should not grant this commission of investigation on this kind of a foundation. Let me say that there are two grounds, and only two possible grounds, that occur to me which can justify motions of this kind or debates of this class in the House. The first is that they are undertaken for the public good, for the raising of the tone of public morality and public life in this country.
Hear, hear.

I take it from the feeble 'hear, hear ' that there are at least some members of the opposition who claim that this is the ground upon which this debate has been carried on. Well, we of the Liberal party cannot have the slightest objection to the results along that line because I say deliberately that I do not think that when the statement of the minister is carefully and calmly read from beginning to end it will be considered any misfortune for the Liberal party that he was allowed to make the magnificent defence _ of his conduct to which this House has listened. I have just a little suspicion as to how far the public good is really paramount in the minds of my hon. friends on the opposition side when I reflect on the somewhat chastened countenances which they displayed when that statement was made. That chastened appearance would be much more easily explained if the second possible cause to which I wish to refer was more immediately in their mind when they moved this resolution and set in motion this debate. If they were not actuated by a desire for the public good, then there is' only one other purpose which could have moved them and that was to secure a party advantage by discrediting the good name of the people of Canada and the public life of the country in the person of a chosen minister of

the majority of the people. I know that members on the opposition side are a litle touchy when any reference is made to the result of the last election. My hon. and agreeable friend from Elgin (Mr. (brothers), I think it was, grew very warm in a recent debate on this subject, and asked whether the last election was to be held as an approval of all that had taken place in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. If I am in order in answering that question, I should like to say that having talked with many electors in that part of the country I have the honour to represent, the verdict in the general elections, in my judgment at any rate, conveyed a disapproval of a campaign of that kind. I am convinced, from private and personal intercourse with many people not of the Liberal party, that the result might have gone the other way if the opposition had based their fight upon a policy instead of the class of fight they put up. My hon. friend from St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) took a very prominent part in that contest and he came to my constituency.
Order.

I think this has a very distinct bearing on the question before the House. I am examining into the motives which underlie this resolution and I think that what I am saying is strictly pertinent. In any case, I can gratify my hon. friend by saying that however disagreeable it may be to them, there will not be very much more of it. My hon. friend from St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) came to my constituency. He came, so far as I know, in a perfectly honourable way, accompanied by some unusual apparatus-an apparatus never required by William Pitt or Gladstone and which our own Prime Minister has hitherto not needed to enthuse the audiences he is in the habit of addressing. I must say that I do not think the class of campaign carried on by my hon. friend there did any good to the Conservative party. I had ample evidence only last evening, that many members of the House, when they want to see moving pictures go to Bennett's theatre, and I have every reason to believe that when they want to heaT good public speaking they will go to an orderly conducted public meeting.
I shall vote against the motion to appoint an investigating committee because I believe in the first place, that to use the power of appointing such a committee on frivolous grounds would encourage the appointment of similar committees every day in the week. If you take the affidavit of a man, who has been described in terms which were not greatly objected to even on the opposition benches, as your basis for appointing a committee of investigation, you can get such men by the dozen in every constituency who will make affidavits to defame the character of members on either side. I shall vote against the resolution in the second place, because, in my judgment, to appoint such a committee, except upon the very strongest ground, derogates from that public esteem which deservedly is attached to the high and responsible position of a minister of the Crown. A minister of Crown is the result of years of hard and honest service to the people in whatever county he lives. That position is the result of constant service to the people, and, as a general rule, of many contested elections, and you will lower that high position and very great responsibility in the public estimation if you appoint an investigation committee, such as is now asked for, except upon the very strongest possible grounds. In the third place, I shall vote against this motion because the only ground urged for the appointment of such a committee is the affidavit furnished by a man self confessed and proved to be a disgruntled seeker of government favours. I shall never give a vote in this House with a clearer conscience-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
CLARK-with a clearer conscience that what I am doing is in the best interests of the country and the dignity of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I owe it to the House to declare what are the views which the government entertain upon this question and the reasons which have induced them not to accept the motion moved by my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel). I do not intend to discuss in any way the reasons which have been set forth in support of this resolution because I believe that every one of them has been refuted, and triumphantly refuted by my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) concluded a speech, which on the whole was moderate, by the statement that he hoped, as a Canadian, this investigation would be granted, but as a party man that it would be denied. My hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) expressed the same sentiment. He put it a little more emphatically perhaps, and added that if it were the bad fortune of the government and the good fortune of the opposition that the motion would be denied, the people would not fail to visit their disapproval at the proper time. Well, that is a matter of judgment, and I have some claim to my own judgment, and, in the words of my hon. friend who has just addressed the House (Mr. Clark), it is with a perfectly clear conscience and without doubt or hesitation that I say that this motion should not be entertained. This is not the first time unfortunately that the honour of a minister of the Crown has been impugned. Perhaps too frequently for the

honour of this country, motions of this character have been made. This is not the first time a member of this House has thought it his duty to bring charges against a fellow member and sometimes against a minister of the Crown, which, if proved, would drive the member accused out of public life. I agree with my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) that, if the charge that is levelled at my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works in this affidavit were true, he could not remain a member of the government-I do not think he could remain a member of this parliament. But this is not the first time such charges have been made. Whenever a member of this House has thought he owed it to himself and to his position to bring a charge of this kind against a fellow member, he has done it by rising in his place and stating that he was credibly informed and had reason to believe that such and such statements made against that fellow member were true. I quote s.everal precedents, but I will be satisfied with one. Here is the motion made by Mr. Tarte in 1891 against a member of the government of that day:-

Israel Tarte, Esq., the member representing the electoral district of Montmorency in this House, having declared from his seat in the House that he is credibly informed and that he believes he is able to establish by satisfactory evidence

Then follow the statements of fact. Is this the method followed by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel)? That hon. gentleman has this affidavit in his hand, this sworn declaration which was read most solemnly at a public meeting by no less a person that the premier of New Brunswick, making certain charges against the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). But though the hon. member (Mr. Daniel) has this document in his hand, does he dare to say that he is credibly informed that these accusations against my hon. friend are true? Does he dare to say that he has reason to believe them true? No, he does not take that responsibility. He incorporates th'at affidavit in a motion which he places before the House, but he has not sufficient faith in the statements of the affidavit to declare that he believes them true, and that he can prove the facts therein alleged. I am not surprised that my hon. friend the member for the city of St. John will not, even with this affidavit, say that he is credibly informed that the facts therein alleged can be substantiated by evidence. This affidavit bears on its face the evidence of falsehood,-I do not think I am speaking too strongly when I say so. In the first place, it is the evidence of a man, who, if we are to take his word, is a self-confessed boodler. What faith will you place in the words of a man who makes a Sir WILFRID LATJRIER.
charge against another, but who cannot make that charge without accusing himself? Do hon. gentlemen on the other side place very much faith in the statement of a man who thus comes before the House and confesses his own turpitude? If they place any faith in a story of that kind, they have the faith that will move mountains. But I do not think they should make allegations against any hon. member of this House upon such an affidavit as that.
Let us go into the statements in this affidavit and see what it discloses. Mr. Mayes states that on a certain occasion he entered into a contract with Mr. McAvity. I do not characterize that contract in any way. He said that when he made that contract with Mr. McAvity he paid $2,000 to the Minister of Public Works. This allegation is not new, it has been before the public for four months at least. It has been discussed by the press in all its bearings, and we know all about it. The Minister of Public Works, when that charge was made, met it immediately by admitting frankly that, in October, 1905, he had received money from Mr. Mayes, but said that it was money honestly paid to him for legal services. Mr. Mayes in his affidavit states-No, he does not state, but insinuates-that the money was not for professional service but for political influence. Now, we are men of common sense in this House: does anybody believe, after what we know of Mr. Mayes and the matter he has been prosecuting in an effort to help his own interest, that he would pay $2,000 to any man unless he got consideration for it? If this money was paid for political services where were these services rendered? This contract for dredging was given openly and squarely, without possibility of influence from anybody; it was given upon tender openly called for, and the contract was awarded to the' lowest tenderer who happened to be Mr. Mayes. What opportunity was there to use political influence? Yet, that is the charge made against the Minister of Public Works. On one side we have the statement of a self-confessed boodler that he paid this money for political services and on the other we have the statement of an honest man that the money was paid for legal services. Which are we to believe? Are we, under these circumstances, to take anything out of this affidavit? It would be a different thing if the hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) had risen in his place and said: I have reason to believe that these statements are true. He does not say so, but simply lays this document upon the table of the House. His statement, in effect, is:	I have not sufficient faith to believe this affidavit upon

it, but we want the House to take action upon it. That is something new to our procedure and is not consistent with the rules and precedents of this House. The affidavit goes on to say that all this was before the Minister of Public Works had become a member of parliament or a minister of the Crown of the Dominion, but that since my hon. friend became a member of the government he had held up Mr. Mayes for the payment of moneys due to him. On this part of the case, I altogether agree with the words spoken by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) that if there has been a holdup it was not a holdup of Mr. Mayes by the Minister of Public Works, it was the case of Mr. Mayes trying to hold up this minister of the Crown. The facts are before the House in the documents that have been brought down. There is the letter by Mr. Mayes to the Minister of Public Works, and the letter by the Minister of Public Works in reply, showing that when, upon one occasion, Mr. Mayes was pressing the minister for the payment of money, he stated, in effect:	Unless I receive my money immediately, and moreover, unless you take over my dredge at a certain price, I will hold you up. He followed that up with threats to the minister, trying to induce the minister to buy his dredge. This was a clear attempt at a holdup. But the Minister of Public Works, answering like the honest man that he is, said that he would have nothing to do with it, and showed Mr. Mayes the door. And then Mr. Mayes went to the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick.
Reference has been made to the Hodgins case, and the question is asked: Why does not the Prime Minister do in this case what he did in the Hodgins case? When Mr. Hodgins made his statement in the press I thought it my duty to refer it to the chief commissioner of the Transcontinental Railway, and that gentleman asked for an investigation. Does it not strike hon. gentlemen opposite that there is a difference between the case of Mr. Hodgins and the case oi this man? Mr. Hodgins did not accuse himself, he accused some one else, he accused the commissioners. Mr. Hodgins, I think, is an honest man. He stated that there had been something wrong going on in the classification on the Transcontinental Railway. Believing that to be the statement of an honest man, I thought it my duty to call the attention of the commissioner to it, and the commissioner finding that his action was called in question, asked at once for an investigation. But are we to be told by hon. members opposite that whilst it is logical, whilst it is right to take action upon the statement of an honest man, we must take the same action upon the statement of a self-confessed boodler?
I see a great difference between the two cases.. So with the case of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). That hon. gentleman, to his credit be it said, when he saw a statement in a respectable newspaper reflecting upon himself, thought it was his duty at once to take action. But this again is a different case altogether, and I repeat that I refuse to be carried away by the statement of Mr. Mayes, unless his statement is corroborated by some other witnesses.
There is another consideration. This is the first time, as I have said, that we have such a motion made in this matter. The hon. member for the city of St. John has taken a course different from any other that has been taken under similar circumstances. I go further, and say that the hon. member for St. John has made it impossible for the government or any supporter of the government to accept his motion. This is a motion made on going into Committee of Supply, it is a motion which, according to the rules of the House we cannot amend. There is a statement in this motion referring to a past action. The House should not be called upon to investigate under any circumstances the conduct of a man who was not a member of this House. I think this is according to the rules of the House. If we wanted to. limit that inquiry, we could not do it. The rules of the House do not allow us to take a syllable from that motion, and do not allow us to add a syllable to it. We must take it as it is, holus bolus, swallow it all or deny it all. Well, undei such circumstances the only thing left for us to do, even if the substance of the motion under other circumstances warranted action, is to deny it altogether. But the last and supreme consideration is that this is a motion of want of confidence.
