I would not press that argument under different circumstances; but in the present case, we are not disposed to vote want of confidence in the Minister of Public Works for the reason that we are proud of him, and this evening we are prouder of him than ever before. I have frankly stated to the House the reasons why we cannot accept this motion.

Before reviewing the reasons given by my right hon. friend why he and those who sit behind him cannot accept this motion, I wish to say a word with reference to Mr. Mayes. I do not know whether my right hon. friend personally knows Mr. Mayes or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I never saw him.

I do not know whether the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) personally knows Mr. Mayes or not. But any one can easily see that unless there is a personal knowledge, it is quite possible to do a very great wrong to a private citizen

who is not able to defend himself on the floor of the House, and to do it under the shadow of the privilege of a member of parliament. Therefore I take the very first opportunity of saying that I know Mr. Mayes very well, I have known Mr. Mayes for a long period of years, and I know nothing to the discredit of Mr. Mayes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not even this?

I know nothing to the discredit of Mr. Mayes. If you take Mr. Mayes as a citizen, I think he is just as reputable, has just as good a character, and stands just as high as the Minister of Public Works, and I am not saying anything to the disparagement of the Minister of Public Works in saying that. Mr. Mayes is a business man who, on the streets of St. John, or on the streets of any other city, enjoys a credit as good and his word is as good, as the credit or the word of the Minister of Public Works, and in saying that I am not saying anything to the discredit of the Minister of Public Works. Mr. Mayes is a self-made man, he has conquered hard circumstances, he has made a place for himself, he has made a certain patrimony for himself, and I have yet to find the first man who can point to Mr. Mayes and accuse him of dishonest or dishonourable action in the accumulation of that patrimony. Now I take this opportunity of saying these things because of what I think are the unfounded aspersions that have been made upon his character, made by some gentlemen who confessedly do not personally know him, and therefore have no knowledge upon which they can go.
But my right hon. friend says, do you consider him as good a character as the Minister of Public Works after this affidavit which he has given? Yes, I answer that in the affirmative, Mr. Speaker. Let us now for a single moment, as sensible men, divesting ourselves of party preferences, follow the force of evidence given every day in every court of the land. Here is a man who is brought into the witness box. He is put upon his oath, he is asked questions and he gives answers. He swears to the answers he has given. Maybe before he has got half through his evidence, maybe after he has gone down from the box and others have given evidence, he asks for the privilege to return to the box, or his lawyer asks it for him, and he corrects the evidence which he gave an hour before, or the evidence which he gave the day before. No judge upon the bench, and no lawyer conducting a case, calls that man an infamous liar because he makes a correction. That is a thing which is liable to take place with my right hon. friend, it is liable to take place with myself, it is liable to. take place with any man. Now if that be true, no one has a right to call a man an infamous liar when he is not in Mr. FOSTER.
his place, because he swears to a statement, and afterwards corrects it. For instance, he had in his mind a certain thing, his lips formed that, and his pen followed the direction of his mind, and a date was written down which he fully believed was the date he intended to have written down. When a few minutes afterwards that is read out by Mr. Hazen, on the platform in the city of St. John, and Mr. Hazen, thinking that the date is wrong, turns to the gentleman and queries as to the date, and is instantly told, 1905, that 1905 was the date he intended. When he finds 1907, as against 1905 which he intended, he immediately writes a letter to the gentleman who is chiefly interested, and in that letter says, it was 1905 I meant, and not 1907. That letter informed the Minister of Public Works, that letter became public property and informed the public of Canada. When a man under these circumstances made an error-he did not intend to make the error-he did not himself make the error-is it quite fair for an hon. member protected by the privileges of parliament, to call him an infamous liar? I cannot take that view of it nor can any sensible man who knows what goes on in business, on the street, in courts of law every day and almost every hour. A great deal has been made of that. The Minister of Public Works said:	Why did not the reporters
hear it ? I put this simple question to my right hon. friend. At a large meeting of this kind, where there was more speaking than any reporter could take, would a shorthand reporter take down that long affidavit as it was read? No body thinks that. Why did not the reporters take it? Because the reporters said to themselves, there is a typewritten copy of the affidavit, we will take what we can of the speeches, that affidavit will be given to us and we will have it for out papers. In that typewritten copy of the affidavit which was signed by Mr. Mayes the date was 1907 because Mr. Hazen, when he read it, did not take his pencil and change the figure from seven to five

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How could he change another man's affidavit?
I suppose it would have been stated

Does it not strike the hon. member that the explanation which the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Daniel) said was made at the moment would strike the reporters as well as anybody else and would be such a marked thing that they would make a note of it?

My hon. friend thinks he has put a very important question. What idea would present itself to the mind of a reporter in the hurry of an important meeting when an affidavit was being read,

of the whole purport of that affidavit? He did not know when some one said: ' Is that date correct,' and another answered: ' 1905;' it would go in at the ear but it was not a thing which a reporter would take down. The reporter would look to the document itself and he would give that to his paper.
I do not think there is any doubt about that and to the man who will try to imagine the actual circumstances, that will commend itself as a reasonable explanation of this error getting into the newspapers instead of being corrected there and then.
What matter on earth is it whether it was 1907 or 1905? For the space of a few hours the Minister of Public Works had a grievance because there was going abroad in the press a statement that he received money in 1907 when he actually received it 1905. To that extent it was a hardship upon my hon. friend and he had a perfect right to complain of it and make what he could of it, but to the man who went to the affidavit itself and analysed it, it did not make a pin's difference whether it was 1907 or 1905 as far as the personal action of the Minister of Public Works was concerned. The other fact is that following straight on the heels of the 1907 issue came the correction of 1905. You can make what grievance you like of that, I think the Minister of Public Works tried to make that his whole case in order to create sympathy for himself as a much-abused and much-maligned man. It was not in keeping with my hon. friend's abilities, standing and experience as a public man. It seems to me it would have been far better to say:
* Well, I was grievously wronged by that date being given as 1907 when it should have been 1905, but this man made a mistake, he corrected that mistake as soon as he knew it had occurred, and within 12 or 15 hours the whole country got the right statement of the case and had it alongside of the other.' Thus, I think undue stress has been laid upon that matter.
Let me now check off for a moment the reasons given by my right hon. friend as to why this motion should not be adopted. He says the government are precluded from allowing the motion to pass because it is made as a want of confidence motion. Are we to go over that old ground again and again? How often has my right hon. friend himself, the leader of this government, accepted and voted for motions which have been made as want of confidence motions if every amendment to Supply is to be considered a want of confidence motion. My hon. friend knows that he has accepted them again and again. He can accept this just as easily as he could accept the half dozen others which he accepted in the last parliament and allowed to be carried without challenging a vote, in some cases saying that he accepted the motion. These 139
motions were consequently passed, and then by the proper mechanism we returned to the consideration of Supply. My right hon. friend therefore is not opposing this motion because it is moved as an amendment to Supply. Am I out of order in saying that the objection which he raises on that score is a herring trailed across the track in order to take away the sense of smell from the real objection of the right hon. gentleman, his real objection being that he does not believe the motion should be allowed to pass under any consideration. My right hon. friend will not deny that that is the position he takes, he does not believe the motion should pass under any consideration. Why? Well he says that no member on this side of the House has had the hardihood or the courage to get up and say: ' I myself as a member of the House take the responsibility of charging the minister,'-and that consequently this motion was not properly brought before the House.
Will my right hon. friend quote me a parliamentary rule which makes it necessary that a member in proferring his motion to the House for whatever purpose, is bound to take that line. I have heard the Speaker say that is a rule of the House. I have heard other gentlemen over and over again declare the same, and declare that we are not in earnest because we do not take that method. But, the main point is the essence of the thing that we want investigated. The manner in which we shall have it brought before the House in order to get an investigation is within the choice of the member himself, so lotng as he conforms to the rules of the House. It will not go down with this House and it will not go down with this country, that simply because of a form which does not agree with the opinion of my right hon. friend, that therefore the substance shall not be investigated. What we want to do is to have the substance investigated, and the substance is very material indeed. Let me exhaust the two examnles my right hon. friend has given. He sees no analogy at all between the Hodgins case, the Em-merson case, and this case. I admit that the analogy is not complete because to my mind this is a stronger case than either of the others. In the Hodgins case you have simply a series of newspaper articles; you have no affidavit. But savs my right hon. friend: I choose to consider that Mr. Hodgins is an honest man ; I do not choose to consider that Mr. Mayes is an honest man, and therefore I will take a simple letter written by Mr. Hodgins, whom I consider to be an honest man, rather than take the sworn statement of Mr. Mayes, whom I do not consider to stand in that light. That is a mere matter of taste. My right hon. friend had no right to order an investigation into the Hodgins case simply because



he thought or did not think that Mr. Hod-gins was an honest man ; the point was, what was the accusation conveyed in what Mr. Hodgins said, and, whether Mr. Hod-gins was an honest man or not, if the accusation was one which made against what was improper in administration and government, my right hon. friend as premier of this country is bound to take it up and have it investigated. But let me press once more upon my right hon. friend this fact : my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is an influential and able and experienced lawyer; he is able to conduct his own case; he has not been foreign to libel suits for, if my memory serves me right, he has threatened several and brought some. Does my right hon. fiiend think it is reasonable that if the Minister of Public Works had an unimpeachable case he would allow that which he designated as the foulest outrage which could be done to any public man, to be put in the form of an affidavit where the man brought himself within the grip of the law and the toils of justice; does my right hon. friend think he would allow that to lie there undisturbed for four months and suffer and sweat under the grossest slander that a public man in this country has had inflicted upon him, and never issue a writ, never make a single step forward towards punishing the dastardly outrage which was perpetrated against him as he has declared over and over again in this House? My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has a good deal of the courteous and of the amiable about him, but he also has some human nature, and the man who could so righteously and indignantly declare against this outrage and the perpetrator of it is a human being by the very indignation that he shows. And it would be his very first impulse to say: 'I will show that man that I can keep my reputation; if there is any law in this country I will take him before the courts and I will preserve my character.' That, the Minister of Public Works has not done. But if he thinks that Mr. Mayes is below his rank, which I beg leave to doubt, the Hon. Mr. Hazen is equal with him in every respect; in point of public view, in point of private character, and the Hon. Mt. Hazen laid himself open when he read the fabricated- what was it that my hon. friend here behind me called it-a 'promulgated' falsehood?

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member (Mr. Poster) has mistaken what I said. What T did say was (and I tried to speak grammatically), that he had promulgated a false affidavit. It may be foreign English to my hon. friend, but that is not my fault.

I owe my learned and cultured friend from Red Deer a debt of Mr. FOSTT R.
gratitude which I am afraid I will never be able to repay, for this much needed instruction which he has been good enough to give me to-night. But here is the premier of the province of New Brunswick who in a public assembly, in the eye and in the hearing of this Dominion of Canada, read this promulgated falsehood and by still further promulgating it and giving it further currency added to the gravity of the outrage perpetrated upon the Minister of Public Works. And the Minister of Public Works wants us to think that he is of such angelic and such seraphic disposition that he lies quietly under the double-promulgated falsehood and does not take action. Well, it seems to me that we have got to have a great deal of that faith which my hon. friend from Red Deer has in ministerial dignity and ministerial excellence, to quite reconcile these matters one with the other. Now, let us take these two cases; I have traced to a certain extent the case of Mr. Hodgins, and my right hon. friend thought that should be investigated, and he appointed a commission and it was investigated. Take the case of Mr. Emmerson. Did my right hon. friend commit an injustice, or allow a man to commit an injustice against himself, in the case of Mr. Emmerson? Did he rise when that allusion was made in this House and say: ' If any man in this House will stand up and declare that he is credibly informed thus and so, and charges the minister then he shall have an investigation at once?' The Prime Minister did not do that Why was it? Was it that the then minister was of a different mould, of a little more sensitive nature, and felt he ought to relieve his colleagues of any possible imputation that might come upon them, and that therefore out of his generosity he sacrificed himself when no man stood up in this House and made a charge against him? Or was it because my right hon. friend procured the resignation of the then minister without demanding that a single man in opposition should have the courage to get up and pledge his seat? These two cases do not hold water when compared with the action of my right hon. friend in this case. Why the difference? If my right hon. friend wishes this motion not to pass, but still wishes an investigation we will not stand upon the order in which it goes. We will not tie ourselves to any particular amendment or any particular mode. Let my right hon. friend have the investigation and he may make the investigation upon whatever method or plan he likes. All we ask for is the investigation. Suppose Mr. Mayes had a seat in this House, suppose he sat here by my side, suppose he did not make an affidavit, did not make a declaration, but simply rose as a member and stated what he had stated

in his affidavit, my hon. friend would grant an investigation. Why ? From the mere mechanical fact that the man who made the statement happened to be here in this House, while the man who made the affidavit is not in this House. Does some one say 'character'? Would his character have been any better if he had been sitting here in this House than it would be if he were on the streets of St. John? Does not my right hon. friend see that this is simply switching straws? There is the absolute affidavit of a man who is just as reputable and just as honourable on the streets of St. John as he would be if he happened to be a member of this House. But my right hon. friend swings clear of another thing. He says that Mayes was a self-confessed bood-ler. Suppose my right hon. friend takes this view of the question. Suppose it comes to be a matter of common notoriety that if a man will enjoy the patronage of the government he has to have a pull to get it. Suppose he cannot get it unless he gets the pull, there is the compulsion of circumstances to make a man league himself with one who has the pull in order to get the work which he ought, as a free Canadian, to get in competition and without pull at all. Well, Sir, suppose that happens to be the case. I will tell you cases that I know of. I know of case after case where, in order to carry out the business that had been formerly carried out, a Conservative has to league himself with a Liberal and lie as a silent partner in order that the Liberal may get from the government the employment, the contracts, the work which is denied him in open and fair competition. That is an undoubted fact. Over and over and over again that is proved.
Will the hon. gentleman cite an instance of that?
Oh, my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) must not be quite so fresh.

Order, order.
Mr. FOSTER, Then, shall I say soft? My hon. friend must not think I am to be switched off from my argument by a remark which is not at all pertinent in this case. I do not say it was impertinent, though that could be applied to a remark but not to a person.
May I ask again if the hon. member will cite an instance to prove what he says?
My hon. friend puts to me the question if I will cite an instance. At this time I will not cite an instance.
Hear, hear.

Now, will my hon. friend answer me a question? What inference does he dTaw from my answer?
139i
That the hon. gentleman is not very well able to prove his own statement.
I will say to my hon. friend that I am very well able to prove it over and over again when I wish to and as I wish to. Now, Mr. Speaker, where was I when this

Oh, oh.
Mr. FOSTER-mild friend of mine broke in upon me in such an unaccustomed way? My right hon. friend stated that Mr. Mayes was a self-convicted boodler. Did my right hon. friend sense, when he stated that, what characterization he would have to make of Mr. McAvity, the bosom friend of the Minister of Public Works? My right hon. friend did not think of that. If Mr. Mayes was a self-convicted boodler, Mr. McAvity would be that ten times over and he has been caught with the boodle on him. No man in this House can deny that Mr. McAvity, acting with what my right hon. friend calls a self-convicted boodler, has taken out of the treasury of the country $35,900 for which he dug no mud. For all that Mayes got he did actual work. Now my right hon. friend sees how dangerous it is to play with phrases looking only to one side and seeking only for his own advantage. I call upon him as leader of the government and keeper of the treasury to go after Mr. McAvity and to get the peoples' money back. Mr. McAvity was the tempter, if there was any temptation, of Mr. Mayes. It was Mr. McAvity who engineered the transaction, it was Mr. McAvity who said: * Come along; I am going up to Ottawa; meet me there.' He came with an introduction given to him by the present Minister of Public Works. Now, let it be known that the Minister of Public Works and Mr. McAvity were not strangers who had met in 1905 for the first time. Mr. McAvity was at one time the president and a director of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, appointed thereto by my hon. friend, paid therefor by my hon. friend, and all the time that he was president and director having the patronage of the railway in the matter of such supplies as appertained to his particular line of business. My hon. friend therefore knew him, employed him, put him in positions of trust, saw that the patronage went to him and he was well acquainted with him in party and political matters. They were brothers together; they were bosom friends. Did my right hon. friend think, when he used that pet phrase of his, that he was thereby giving his own characterization of this gentleman so trusted by the Minister of Public Works, so favoured by that minister and who profiited so well out of the public chest, as he did in this instance? My right hon. friend forgets that phase of the question, and that is the phase in which the people are most interested. That is the very

crux of this resolution, and we want an investigation to know just how much money Mr. McAvity got; how he got it; what influences he brought to bear in order to get it, and how it came to be so easy in that department for a man to procure a contract from it for another and then draw from it this $35,900. That is what the people want to know. The right hon. gentleman never had a truer friend than the editor of the St. John 'Globe.' I do not know that he has a truer friend to-day. The editor of the St. John ' Globe ' does not see any particular virtue in Mr. McAvity's rake-off of $35,933. My right hon. friend has other good friends in the old Liberal party. Let him read what the press is saying to-day. Let him take his own papers that support him loyally and truly, and let him read their straightforward, honest declarations to-day. To-morrow morning when the news floats out on the wires and is read by the people that an investigation was refused on the flimsy pretext that no man got up and on his honour said he was prepared to prove this sort of thing, or on the equally flimsy pretext that the resolution was moved as an amendment to Supply, and, therefore, was a want of confidence motion, and when it goes out to the people that, according to the statement of the Minister of Public Works, Mr. McAvity did a proper thing when he took the $35,900, that he cannot be proceeded against, that no law in this country can take this money from him- let the right hon. gentleman believe that when that statement of his minister goes out. and his own refusal to investigate the matter, it will be hard reading for many of his best friends, and will not be a thing of which this country of ours can be proud. I do not know that it is necessary for me to say anything more on this matter. I have simply to make one plea more to my right hon. friend, and that is to give free course for investigation in this parliament. When matters of this gravity are brought up, at least allow the people, whose affairs we are transacting, the slight privilege of a fair examination. You have one man making a certain statement on his word; you have another making a contrary statement on his oath, and you are in doubt between the two. Why is it not a proper thing to have an investigation where both can be taken on oath? Is there anything wrong or unfair in that? Let my right hon. friend tell me of one interest that will be injured if he grants this committee? If the Minister of Public Works took that $2,000 and took it as a solicitor's fee, it will be any easy matter to bring him before the committee and ask him to show his books, bills and receipts and checks and question him upon them. With all my deep admiration for the splendid dignity of a minister of the Crown, I still think that sometimes it is better to have these things Mr. FOSTER.
established on oath as is done in suits at law and vexed questions before the courts. It seems to me that no judge would turn out, no lawyer would ask to debar from giving evidence a man who was an accomplice in the thing charged. Every day in our courts of law such men are relied upon as witnesses. So that I make my plea to my right hon. friend that if there is no interest which will be injured, if the Minister of Public Works, who declares his innocence in such indignant tones, is really innocent, then that can be easily proved before the committee. If the affidavit made is false, that can be proved and the man who swore to a falsity can be punished. What interest would be injured by sending this matter to a committee and having it fully investigated?
Am I to understand the Minister of Public Works denies having received the $2,000?
No, as I understand it, he admits having received it, but what he says is that it was for professional services.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Mayes says it was for very different services. Mayes swears to his statement and we have the word of the minister denying it. But it would be more satisfactory if both these men were brought where they would be sworn and cross questioned and the truth brought out by examination of their books and checks and the like. Therefore, I again press upon the Prime Minister, that if no interest would be injured in the matter, let the people have the chance to know the truth by a full, free and impartial investigation.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sure that, at this late hour and at this stage of the debate, no one could hope to add anything new, by way of information, to the subject which has been so thoroughly discussed all this afternoon and evening. All that I care to do is to try to emphasize two or three points, which seem to be the points of vital importance, and which have been fully covered by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works in his admirable address, but which it would be well to emphasize again. But first let me say a word or two on the general question of investigations. I-believe that the people will distinguish carefully, as they have done in the past, between motions which are made for the bona fide purpose of investigation and motions made purely and simply for the purpose of manufacturing political capital ; and the manner in which these different classes of motions may be made from time to time will have much to do with enabling the public to distinguish between the two.

Mr. 8PROULE. I rise to a point of order. Has the hon. gentleman the right to impute motives with regard to a motion before the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no rule to prevent my imputing motives.
I think there is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There might be an objection to imputing improper motives, but I am sure my hon. friend will not labour to find an authority to say that I may not impute motives. I may impute to the hon-gentleman some highly honourable motives, and that would not be contrary to the rules of parliament. Sir, I have in this case imputed no motives, I have only drawn a distinction between two classes of demands for investigation. And I wish to consider that point as illustrated by what we have now before us. Now, this matter of the Mayes' affidavit is not something which transpired to-day or yesterday; it transpired many months ago. My hon. friend from the city of St. John, and all those who have been interested in the matter, have had these documents in their possession for many months; and if they had desired an investigation they have had abundant opportunity to seek it in a different way and at an earlier stage of the session when the House ^could have dealt with it. But, for their own purposes, they have not sought that; for their own purposes, they have kept these documents in their pockets, or- Mr. LENNOX. If the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) will allow me a question: Is he aware that the papers in connection with this matter were moved for and that they were only brought down eight days ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is referring to papers of a different character from this. The Mayes' affidavit was not moved for in this House. That affidavit is the basis of these proceedings and it has been in the hands of my hon. friends for months, and they have had every opportunity to challenge investigation if they had so desired. I want to invite the attention of the House and the country to the different forms of procedure in the matter of investigation. I had occasion to do so recently in the case of another subject that we were considering, and I wish to treat the same thought to-day. If an hon. member wishes to make a motion for an investigation of any public matter, he can put a notice on the paper setting forth the nature of his proposal, and when it is reached in due course, if the House is disposed to grant an investigation but not to limit it by the particular terms of the motion, an amendment can be moved. Thus, the House can declare in words that are deemed fitting its desire either to have an investigation or not to have an investigation. And, when an hon.
member wishes to make the investigation of a general character, that is the method contemplated by the rules and procedure of parliament. But if a charge is to be made against a minister of the Crown that is a different matter. If an hon. member is prepared to take the procedure illustrated by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to-night, if it be deemed necessary to attack the honour of a minister and charge him with any act of corruption in relation to the matters of which he is a trustee, it is the right of an honourable member to avail himself of the form of motion which is usually a vote of want of confidence and to come forward with a specific charge. And, when this is done, no government would refuse an investigation. But, while that would be the case where a member is prepared to make a specific charge of corruption against a minister, it is not the same when you come to deal with ordinary talk and to demand an investigation of nothing in particular. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) put the case fairly when he said that the honour and dignity of parliament require that we should not order investigations on mere frivolous statements for which there is no strong foundation. And that is the case here to-day; there is no foundation for an investigation. We are concerned in maintaining the honour and dignity of parliament. It happens that one party is in the ascendency to-day; some day another party will be in the ascendency-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) says: 'Hear, hear'. But it will be a long time before my hon. friends of the Conservative party can win by the tactics which they have adopted in this case. There is a manliness, a sense of fair play among the people of Canada which will respond to such statements as those of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) when he shows the dastardly attempts made in the city of St. John to destroy him. I say, we are concerned in maintaining the honour and dignity of parliament; and, if it be laid down as a rule that a member can pick up a statement in a newspaper-whether an affidavit or an editorial article does not matter-and come before the House and say : ' I personally know nothing about this, but I will read it and will move for investigation by a special committee,' we are following a course that is not consistent with the honour and dignity of parliament. But when a motion of that kind is proposed, shall the House accept it? I ask hon. members of both sides to think seriously of the view I present. So, we have this motion in the form of a non-confidence motion. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Fos-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. McAvity, as appears, says he was engaged in a business transaction which was right and proper and one which he is prepared to defend. But, whatever may be said about Mr. McAvity, Mr. Mayes by his own affidavit declares that he entered into an improper, corrupt arrangement for the purpose of extorting from the Dominion of Canada money which he could not lawfully receive. You may hold Mr. McAvity in suspense-I offer no opinion at this moment as to his nqsition. But I say that Mr. Mayes, by his own statement, in his own affidavit, declares that he entered into what he meant to be a corrupt arrangement whereby he might, as my hon. friend said, filch this money from the public treasury.
It took two to make a bargain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very good. The second party is not in dispute, we have yet to know what is the fact with regard to the second. But I am judging Mr. Mayes by his own affidavit, and I say that by his own statement in his own affidavit he puts himself in a position which must be exceedingly painful to every man who would like to call himself his friend.
Why not then take Mc-Avity's evidence in favour of Mayes, if you are going to take it the other way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friends had been really anxious to have an investigation, we would have heard of it a long time ago. Now let us come to what I regard as the two important points in this discussion; and first, the affidavit. Why, my hon. friend from St. John says, it was a mistake. The affidavit had in it a certain date, 1907. He admitted that rather reluctantly, but

pressed by the Minister of Public Works he admitted it.
No reluctance about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am bound to accept the hon. gentleman's statement. At all events, he had that affidavit in his possession and he claims now there was a mistake made in it as to a given date. The hon. member for North Toronto spent considerable time in aTguing that it made no difference at all; what difference did it make whether it was 1907 or 1905? Why, Mr. Speaker, it made all the difference in the world. The date was the essence of the whole thing. A document saying that in the year 1907 the contractor Mayes gives Dr. Pugsley, the Minister of Public Works at that time, $2,000-that was a thing that would startle the country. But when you change the date to 1905, what value had the affidavit? What concern could it have been to a public gathering in the city of St. John to know that two years before, as between Mr. Mayes, the client, and Dr. Pugsley, the lawyer, there had been some business transaction involving the payment of fees?

Does the minister forget that if the statement made by Mr. Mayes were true, that the transaction occurred say in 1905 instead of 1907. that then, under the statute, the party who was guilty of it, the present Minister of Public Works, was guilty of a crime which would render him liable to seven years' imprisonment, and therefore he would be a criminal, and could not be a member of this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not know that. If my hon. friend says it is so, I am not going to deny it.
In that affidavit, as I heard it read, is it not clearly stated that Mr. Hyman was the Minister of Public Works at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; but let us consider the circumstances under which the affidavit was produced. We had an election in the city of St. John. Mr. Hyman was not a candidate; the hon. gentleman who is now the Minister of Public Works was the candidate; and it was to damage the Minister of Public Works of to-day, it was to damage Dr. Pugsley, and try to elect the hon. gentleman who sits to-day for the city of St. John, that that affidavit was brought forward; and if it had been stated in the beginning that the date in question was 1905, two years before the hon. gentleman became a minister of the Crown, what value would have had that affidavit? The whole value of the affidavit, for the time a'ffi circumstances, was in that date, and that date was given as 1907, and it went out in the press and was circulated the following morning that the Minister of Public Works had received $2,000
from a contractor in a corrupt transaction, while he was a minister of the Crown.
I say again that the whole value of the affidavit was in the date; and if they had brought forward the affidavit at first with the date 1905, it is not nrobable that it would have been read in that meeting at all, because it was absolutely worthless as political capital except they put in a date which would involve my hon. friend in his capacity as Minister of Public Works with that transaction. But what concern was it to the electors of St. John that Mr. Mayes, a well known contractor, and Mr. Pugsley, a well known lawyer, should have had business as between client and legal adviser? Who were concerned in that? Who cared to know whether Dr. Pugsley received $2,000 or $200 for his services? These lawyers in the upper provinces sometimes get very liberal fees. I do not think anybody would say the payment of $2,000 to a gentleman who was the legal adviser of a prominent contractor, was a very large sum. You would not get a big Toronto lawyer to do very much for $2,000. And if it be assumed that because the $2,000 was paid to my hon. friend it is an evidence of corruption, why, any member of the legal profession would say it was utterly preposterous. The whole value of the affidavit turns on the date, and if that affidavit had been sent in with the present date1, 1905, the probability is that it would have been flung out. They would say :	' What do we caTe about
the affairs of Mayes and Pugsley as lawyer and client?' It was only by the falsification of that date, it was only by the insertion of the year 1907 in place of 1905, that the document became of any value politically. It was used with that date in it to damage my hon. friend, and if in the end he escaped damage, no credit is due to the men who used the affidavit in that way.
Now the other feature of the matter which I think is important, is the tenders. Tenders were invited for some dredging, and the specification contained the condition that the party who took the contract must be the owner of a dredge registered in Canada. Two tenders were brought in, Mr. Mayes was the lowest, but Mr. Mayes had not complied with the conditions of the specification. Now, suppose the Minister of Public Works had ignored that defect, suppose he had said. Well, never mind, we will give Mayes the contract all the same. Suppose he had got the contract, I can imagine my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) rising up the following session and saying:	What did
you do? You put in your specification a certain condition, and you therebv shut out from tendering many people who would have tendered, but they could not comply with that condition. Mr. Mayes' tender did not comply with that condition, but you gave him the contract in violation of your

specification-and hon. gentlemen opposite would have been strong in their denunciation of the Minister of Public Works for violating the condition of his own specification. So the Minister of Public Works said: Well, I am going to have difficulty in getting dredges registered in Canada, but I will give everybody a fair chance, I will invite new tenders, and let all have a fair chance. New tenders were invited, and that clause with respect to the dredge being registered in Canada was omitted from the specification. What is wrong with that? I put it to any business man-was not that a fair business arrangement ? Can any man say there was any wrong up to that moment ? Surely not. Then new tenders came in; and it appears that in the meantime Mr. Mayes decided to increase his tender. Can any body find fault with that? When a number of people tender, and their tenders are thrown out and they are asked to tender again, are they all bound to put in the same figures? Surely if the minister has a right to refuse to accept the old tenders, a man who sent in a tender has a perfect right to revise his tender and ask what he pleases. Suppose that in the meantime Mr. Mayes had made up his mind that he had tendered too low,-and we know there are occasions when men do tender too low-suppose that for any reason Mr. Mayes made up his mind that he wanted to get a higher price, and he sent in his tender at a higher figure, in open competition with the world, in response to the invitation, what fault could be found with such a transaction? What is wrong with that up to that point? First the tenders were asked for with a specification as to the dredge. Then it was found that nobody was willing to comply and the department said: 'We will give no favour, we will open the doors to everybody free; ' and they called for new tenders. That is right. When they gave the contract to the man whose tender was lowest.' I submit to any business man in the House that there is nothing wrong in that. We are not concerned in the relations between Mr. McAvity and Mr. Mayes, that is their own business transaction. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says: Why not get the money back from Mr. McAvity. Mr. McAvity got no money from the government, Mr. Mayes was the contractor. Mr. Mayes sent in his tender, he had his association with Mr. McAvity, whether it is good or bad is their own private business. Tenders were called for publicly, tenders were sent in in open competition and the man who offered the lowest price got the work. I submit to the people of Canada who care to interest themselves in the matter that in those few sentences that you have the whole story. It is Mr. Hyman who is accused in this matter. Although the attack is levelled against the present minister (Mr. Pugsley), whatever Mr. FIELDING.
reflection is cast is cast on Mr. Hyman, who is no longer here to defend himself, and unless there are some good grounds for believing, unless somebody is prepared to say on his responsibility, ' I have reason to believe and do believe there was collusion between the minister or the deputy minister or the engineer or somebody ' in that department and that contractor,' I submit there never was a business transaction between the government and contractors that was fairer, straighter or more above-board than the transaction respecting the dredging of the harbour of St. John.

I raised a point of order, Mr. Speaker, on which I did not get your ruling, and I was afterwards contradicted by the hon. member in his speech. I asked your ruling as to whether an hon. member could attribute motives? The Minister of Finance said that the motive of the party who moved this was a political one. I asked your ruling as to whether he could or could not, I have here Bourinot's ' Parliamentary Procedure,' third edition, edited by Dr. T. B. Flint, which says:
No member can be allowed to apply the expression ' impertinence ' to another member, or to attribute motives.
It is upon the strength of that passage that I asked a ruling and on account of the difference between the Minister of Finance and myself and for the direction of the House I would like very much to have your ruling on it.

It is a well-known rule that no improper motive can be attributed.
I did not rule because the Minister of Finance declared he was not imputing any improper motives.
He declared he had a right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A good motive.
A good motive, he facetiously said.
The words are: * Or to attribute motives.'
The intention is that improper motives should not be applied.
If this resolution was only introduced for a political purpose, would it not be for an improper motive and not for the good of the country?
If the tenders were increased in order that a rake-off might be paid for political influence would the Minister of Finance hold that that was not a corrupt arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the tenders were open to the public, if there was free, open competition without collusion, they are not

called upon to inquire into the motive which led any man to increase his tender.

Without reference to the other tenders, if the tender was increased in order that a rake-off might be paid to a man for political purposes, would the minister say that that was not a corrupt arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Everything would depend on whether there was collusion or not. If a matter is open to public tender and a man sends in a tender to-day at a dollar and then further tenders are called for and he sends in a second tender at $1.50, I say that if he gets the contract because he is the lowest tenderer in fair and open competition, without any collusion or any allegation of collusion, there is no ground foT inquiring into the reason which led him to make an increase in his tender.
